subsubtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY-SUPPORT FOR AIMS AND OBJECTIVES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today marks the fiftieth anniversary of the Commonwealth, a unique association of 44 countries of different racial, cultural, and economic backgrounds. At a time when the international community is engulfed in a crisis of mistrust and inaction, the Commonwealth has the facility to bring diverse nations together in harmony and good will. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That Canada renew its support of the aims and objectives of the Commonwealth, particularly the dedication of the Commonwealth to upholding human rights, opposing racial discrimination, and resolving the world economic crisis through measures to close the rich-poor gap in the world.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, news reports today confirm that the minister responsible for the status of women has been unable to influence cabinet to initiate an independent review of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. He is reportedly getting pretty tired of dealing with women lobbying for changes in the Constitution and for changes to restore integrity to the advisory council. In dismissing these representations, the minister has also cynically observed that the women's movement, for which he is supposed to be responsible, is easily manipulated. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That this House calls upon the Prime Minister to relieve the present minister responsible for the status of women from his tiresome duties and replace him with a person who will have the confidence and respect of women and of cabinet.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

I am just welcoming him to his seat.
I should like to ask the minister when was the government first informed of President Reagan's decision to abandon unilaterally the east coast fisheries treaty and, further, what immediate steps the government took, either publicly or privately, to convey to the Americans Canada's profound opposition to this move.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EAST COAST TREATY-NOTIFICATION OF WITHDRAWAL FROM CONSIDERATION BY UNITED STATES SENATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was telephoned by Secretary Haig-I believe it was on Tuesday evening of last week-to inform me that he would be recommending to the President that the administration not proceed with the east coast fisheries treaty but that it do proceed with the east coast boundaries agreement. I think we did not receive notification of the President's decision in advance or, if we did, it was so close to the time of his decision that in effect the two came at the same time. I believe that was on Friday. We did not receive any effective advance notice of the President's decision, as I under-

March 9, i 98 i
Oral Questions
stand it, but we did receive advance warning from Secretary Haig that that would be his recommendation.
At the time Secretary Haig called me 1 expressed our profound regret and disappointment at this move, and said that it was not what we had hoped and expected. He informed me that that was true with his side as well, that he had been very optimistic when we had met that he would be able to get it through the Senate, and that it was with great regret that his special negotiator had informed him, after twice discussing it with all the relevant senators, that it was simply impossible to get it through the U.S. Senate. It was on that ground that the American government decided not proceed.
We did not accept the American action. We told the Americans specifically that we were not accepting it in the sense that we did not agree with it, that we protested against it, and that we were profoundly saddened by it.

subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I find it appalling that the minister did not make some public outcry, the moment he was informed of this news, as to how the Canadian public felt and would react to this very distressing move on the part of the American government. However, given the fact that his comments to Secretary Haig were not successful earlier on, can the minister say what steps the government is now proposing to take in the next two days at the very highest levels to persuade President Reagan not to proceed with the announced course he has stated with respect to the east coast fisheries agreement, or will the government simply resign itself to accepting the way in which the American government is proceeding unilaterally?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this was a unilateral decision by the United States without consultation with us. It has been formally announced by the President, and I am not sure there is now any margin for the United States to change that position, especially given the fact that they are only reflecting their belief that they cannot get this through the U.S. Senate and that they cannot get the implementing legislation through either the Senate or the House. We certainly intend to discuss this very fully with the President and to stress especially the importance of conservation of the fish stock, because likely the greatest possible loss in this whole matter is the loss to conservation interests.
It seems that American fisheries officials have not shown themselves capable of adequately protecting fish stocks. This is what troubles us more than any other single thing about the American decision.
We also have their assurance that they will not proceed to enforce U.S. law in the disputed zone against Canadian fishing ships. They will have what is called flag state enforcement, which means we will enforce the law against our ships, they will enforce it against their ships, and either of us can enforce it against ships from third countries. This will avoid the
possibility of a so-called fish war in which each side would be arresting the ships of the other country.

subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE WITH RESPECT TO TREATY

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE WITH RESPECT TO TREATY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, given the situation the minister has now described, what concerns me is whether enough has been done by the government in the past number of weeks to convince the new administration in Washington of the unanimous and intense feeling in Canada against the course it has taken. I cite as an example the fact that on January 17 of this year the Canadian press reported that U.S. foreign relations committee chairman Percy said, after discussions with the Canadian Ambassador, Peter Towe, that he, Senator Percy, felt that treaty changes "can be accepted with reluctance" by Ottawa. He was given to understand that treaty changes can be accepted with reluctance by Ottawa.
I should like to ask the minister what it was in his discussions with Ambassador Towe that led Senator Percy to believe that any changes to the fisheries treaty would be accepted by Ottawa, reluctantly or otherwise, and under what orders was Ambassador Towe acting at the time Senator Percy reached that conclusion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE WITH RESPECT TO TREATY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know the state of Senator Percy's mind at the time he made that statement. In fact our position to the United States all along has been that while we would consider a reduction in the duration of the treaty from one of perpetual duration to one of a limited period of years, say 12, which would probably be long enough to return the capital investment of the fishermen, we would not accept any other changes. In his conversations with me Secretary Haig said that he well understood that the Canadian government would not accept any modifications to the treaty and that that was one of the factors the United States was taking into account in deciding to proceed this way.
The hon. member knows better than most that this treaty was negotiated and signed by the previous U.S. administration, the one with which she was dealing as secretary of state for external affairs. She also had a singular lack of success in convincing the U.S. government to put this treaty through the U.S. Senate.

subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF MARITIME BOUNDARY BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to direct my questions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs as well. He states that what has happened is a unilateral decision, but in effect that unilateral decision was
March 9, 1981

based on a joint decision taken by representatives of the two countries. In fact the East Coast Fishery Resource Agreement signed on March 29, 1979, following negotiations that began in the fall of 1976, which is a long period of time, was designed to establish a Canada-U.S. fisheries commission to provide for co-operative management, and for access and entitlements to specific stocks of mutual concern. At the same time the treaty to submit the delimitation of the maritime boundary in the Gulf of Maine area to binding dispute settlement, provides for the submission of the case to a five-judge chamber of the International Court of Justice for a final decision on the placement of the boundary.
With that background I should like to ask the minister if, in his estimation, the United States is taking the boundary issue to the International Court in order to settle definitively that aspect of negotiations between our two countries before endeavouring to establish the fisheries quotas for conservation methods, or what is his interpretation of these actions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF MARITIME BOUNDARY BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the United States government is prepared to proceed with the boundaries treaty, I understand, which in effect underlies the fisheries treaty. When international arbitration is completed, to a large extent that will effectively settle the fisheries question because it will determine the boundary on either side of which enforcement by the relevant country may take place. The U.S. government believes that there will be no difficulty getting that through the Senate, with its reference to international arbitration.
In the meantime, the U.S. administration is undertaking to try some conservation measures through the New England Fisheries Council. We are told that will not be on the basis of percentages of the catch, as we would prefer, but the U.S. Secretary of State says that it will indicate some interest on the part of the United States government in the preservation of the fisheries. That aspect concerns us a great deal. We would like to see extremely effective conservative measures taken so that the result of this flag state enforcement will not be that fishermen from both sides will be allowed to plunder the stock.
Of course, if the United States is not going to be concerned about conservation, we can hardly say to our fishermen that we are going to restrain them. Then it is the fishing resource that will suffer.

I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. In January, 1977, Canada extended its jurisdiction to 200 miles seaward, and in March of the same year the United States established similar limits. When doing this the United States stated that the principal purpose behind its action was to phase foreign fishermen out of U.S. waters so that the U.S. fishing industry could expand.
Oral Questions
My question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is this: since the United States claims that the March 29, 1979, agreement is inconsistent with its 200-mile legislation, as it guarantees Canadian scallop, herring and groundfish fishermen permanent access to large parts of the United States zone, which is not in a disputed area, is the minister now planning to review all of the bilateral agreements covering fishing operations of foreigners within Canada's 200-mile zone in keeping with the promise made on February 25, 1975, by the then minister of state for external affairs, who is now the Minister of Finance, that the federal government would have the right to reserve for Canadian fishermen that portion of the total resource which they have the capacity to catch in any given year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I completely fail to see how the hon. member's last question affects the previous statement made. In fact, we took the approach that where the line was drawn in fisheries terms was not overly important as long as there was a management of stocks which responded to biology and movement of fish. As long as that possibility existed, obviously our preference was for the treaty as it was negotiated, with great difficulty, because there had to be concessions on both sides. We felt, from the fisheries point of view, that the treaty went a long way to protect the traditional fishing patterns of both Canadian and American fishermen, that it disrupted them as little as possible, and it would produce a management of stocks which would ensure good conservation. I must say the decision which has been announced by the United States worries us from a fisheries point of view in terms of conservation. Certainly I agree with my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that if American fishermen are going to have unbridled access to Georges Bank, then we cannot ask our fishermen to restrain themselves.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister. It also concerns the east coast fisheries treaty. On several occasions in this House, through motions under the provisions of Standing Order 43, we have announced our disapproval of the attitude of the United States toward not ratifying this treaty. I might remind the Prime Minister that the scallop allocation to United States fishermen has increased from about 10 per cent in 1974 to over 40 per cent right now, which is taking away much of the income of the Nova Scotia fishermen.
In view of the visit of the President of the United States tomorrow and on Wednesday, would the Prime Minister give assurances to this House and to the fishermen in Nova Scotia that he will ask the President of the United States to impose a
8020

March 9, 1981
Oral Questions
management plan on the American fishermen fishing scallops and other stocks on the east coast in the area under dispute? Will the Prime Minister ask the President to impose on those American fishermen a quota which will conserve stocks for which Canadian fishermen, in an attempt to do the same thing, are willing to accept regulations imposed by this government and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it would seem that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have dealt with this matter in their previous answers when they indicated that conservation was one of the main preoccupations of this government, and when they indicated the United States administration had undertaken to negotiate, I believe it is with the New England regional council, to ensure that that council would adopt conservation measures compatible with the maintenance of the fish stocks.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext:
With all due respect, Mr. Prime Minister, I will address this question to you.
It has been quite obvious that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this government, in the previous Tory government and in the Liberal government before that, were unable to get those kinds of assurances from the United States. We were not getting any co-operation on that treaty through normal channels, namely, through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of External Affairs. I think it is incumbent upon you now, recognizing the failure-

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext: -of normal channels, that you ask the President of the United States to impose a management plan which will protect those stocks on the east coast. That is not being done now. Will you ask the President of the United States to do something.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext: Are you asking the Speaker a question?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister give an assurance that he, as the Prime Minister of Canada, will request that a management plan be implemented to protect the stocks and income of Canadian fishermen?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say the hon. member is misstating the facts when he says that this government and indeed the United States administration had not endeavoured to ensure that the negotiated treaty would be implemented. On the contrary, we had the assurance from the Carter administration that it would do its best, repeatedly, over a period of two years, to make sure that the treaty was ratified. Therefore, there was on the part of the preceding U.S. administration, our government, and the government of the Leader of the Opposition, an endeavour to obtain ratification of the treaty. What happened in fact is that the U.S. Senate has not ratified the treaty. This government is putting forward the importance of
maintaining friendship with the United States as the basis of the meeting which will take place tomorrow and the next day.
We are presuming that the United States President adopted this course, not because he wants to see an end to the profitable fishing for fishermen of both countries but because he is seeking in some other way to achieve results that are profitable for both countries. In that sense the House must recognize that it is not the U.S. administration that failed to ratify the treaty for the past two years, but the United States Congress. In that sense this government is once again putting the best possible light on the United States action and we are seeking, in a spirit of friendship, with the visit of the United States President to find a solution to this problem.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN SCALLOP ALLOCATION TO U.S. FISHERMEN- REQUEST FOR IMPOSITION OF MANAGEMENT PLAN
speechtext: I would once again request that the Prime Minister raise this with the President.

Madam Speaker, I wish to address my supplementary question on a related matter to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is with regard to the west coast salmon treaty which is now in the process of being negotiated. It will require a great deal of co-operation, trust and good will on the part of both governments in order to become an equitable and fair treaty for both sides. In recognition of the difficulty in getting equitable treatment with regard to the treaty on the east coast, will the minister reconsider the position of the government which guarantees in perpetuity something like 4.5 million Fraser River sockeye and pink salmon to the United States? Will he reconsider the Canadian position on the west coast salmon treaty, which is based on good will?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBIanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in order to help the hon. member understand the previous question, under American legislation the United States Secretary of Commerce can intervene to limit the powers of the regional councils. That is the very question I expect to discuss with Secretary of Commerce Baldridge tomorrow afternoon. If this can be done and if the scallop stocks can be protected through this approach, we might avoid very serious overfishing, which is a threat that now hangs over us.
1 hesitate to link the future of the west coast treaty to the problem on the east coast. We have always resisted playing one against the other. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to protest publicly the American military intervention in support of the junta in El Salvador, and calls on the Prime Minister in his talks with the President of the United States to urge an end to this military involvement on the side of a regressive regime which denies civil rights and is fighting those who wish to establish a democratic government.
He said: Madam Speaker, today, just ahead of the visit of the President of the United States, we are involved in what could become one of the most significant political events of the new administration in the United States. The El Salvadorean situation has all the elements of intensifying not only the crisis within that country but, indeed, could go well beyond that and raise very serious difficulties in the modern world, not only in this hemisphere but everywhere on the planet.
In opening my comments, I want to say that I intend to spend a good part of my time talking about the actual situation in El Salvador, its recent history and its modern reality. For quite plausible reasons I think the people of Canada are not well informed about what is actually taking place in that unfortunate land to the south of us. In so doing, I would like to make it clear that my sources of information on what I am about to say are not, in the main, from Canadian sources, but rather are from American sources. They are from publications like Harpers magazine and The New York Times, from American church leaders as well as from Canadian and El Salvadorean church leaders, from Canadian trade unionists, and finally from a report prepared by the president of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
What is a common characteristic of these groups or individuals? First, all of them have been known historically to oppose authoritarian regimes, whether they are regimes on the left or on the right. They are the people who, in the past, have not hesitated to condemn the Soviet Union's invasion of Afghanistan and, in the present circumstance, they are united in condemning American involvement in El Salvador. Just as they were right in the former case, they are certainly right, as I will argue, in the case of the Americans. What 1 want to stress is that all of these groups, whether church leaders or editors of important American publications, have on their side a distinguished commitment not only to liberty but to the pursuit of truth. Both characteristics are very important, as we will see in this debate on this important situation.
First, I want to say something about the nation of El Salvador. It is important for us to know that it is not only a small country geographically but that it is small in population, somewhere in the neighbourhood of five million people. It is also important for us to know that in that land some 2 per cent of the people own 60 per cent of the arable land. The peasants who make up the vast majority of the population own almost
El Salvador
none of the arable land. In terms of income distribution, 8 per cent of the population receives more than 50 per cent of the national income. In terms of employment opportunities, work, which gives dignity to the daily existence of most men and women, is almost unavailable on a continuing basis for most of the population. In fact, only some 16 per cent of the economically active population is employed throughout the year. For 1979 unemployment averaged 25 per cent. These are some of the crude statistics which describe the present reality of El Salvador.
The history of El Salvador which has led to the present political circumstance which we are debating today is that for nearly 100 years El Salvador has been economically and politically controlled by a handful of families which compose the oligarchy. These families are the owners of the best quality land, which in its production is dedicated not to meeting the needs of the people, in the main, but to serving export markets for coffee, cotton and sugar. This handful of land owners employs a peasant class which is subjected to what can only be described as highly exploitative conditions in terms of modern industrial, northern European and North American experience. Anyone who describes their circumstances in any other terms is misleading.
The traditional oligarchy held direct political power up until the early 1930s. In 1932, as a result of a peasant rebellion which resulted in some 30,000 deaths, the military dictatorship which has oppressed the people up until today was installed in power. Over the past 50 years military government has been followed by military government, serving the interests of the oligarchy, keeping the majority of people out of the political process and systematically blocking all moves in a democratic direction. I will have something more to say about that in light of the observations made by the present American ambassador to the United Nations.
After the Sandinista victory in Nicaragua just a few years ago it was clear that this experience would have far-reaching implications in the region, particularly for those struggling for democracy against tyrannical regimes. Nowhere was this more immediate or apparent than in El Salvador where, on October 15, 1979, a group of young military officers ousted the military dictator, General Carlos Romero. The formation of a civilian military government was announced, and hopes were immediately raised everywhere that the attainment of genuine democracy would not encounter the bitter and bloody resistance which had occurred in Nicaragua. This was particularly the case when a leading social democrat, Manuel Ungo, was nominated by 14 popular organizations to join the five-man ruling junta. Another social democrat, Hector Oqeli, was appointed deputy minister of foreign affairs.
Hopes that the promised, much needed reforms could be implemented were soon dashed. The security forces began new acts of terrorism. The stated objective of the new government had been the democratization of the country, including serious political and economic reforms. However, it soon became

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
evident to the people and the democratic civilian sectors of the government that powerful forces long established in El Salvador would remain opposed to these democratic goals. The rightist sectors of the army grew stronger and eventually displaced the democratically-oriented elements of the army which were in the junta. Once again, repression against the people and violation of human rights became commonplace in El Salvador. At the same time the oligarchy and its allies within and outside the government opposed and blocked, as 1 have said, all attempts at democratic reform. This included assassination of leaders of other political parties.
Then in January, 1980, almost all the civilian members of the government resigned. The hopes that the regime which came into existence just a year and a half earlier had awakened in the land were completely crushed. During the past year the junta, now consisting of only the most reactionary civilians and the military, has continued to exist only by means of military force. The junta has pretended that serious economic reform has taken place. In fact, the so-called reforms have been no more than cosmetic. Instead of genuine human reform, since its beginning in January of last year the current government has provided what has been characterized as "reform by death". That is to say, the fundamental objective of the regime has been the extermination of all opposition through indiscriminate repression and violence on an almost incredible scale.
Robert White, the former United States ambassador, said in an article which I read yesterday in The New York Times the following: "They have killed at a minimum 5,000 or 6,000 kids just on mere suspicion". This inhuman objective of eliminating in a vicious way all opposition was covered up by the so-called reformist agrarian proposals which have been, according to OXFAM and many other groups, a sham. This totally insubstantial land reform policy was matched by another alleged reform of the banking system which, in reality, has left the credit structure of the nation completely unchanged.
What have been the results of such action? They are pretty obvious. They are what one can expect at this point in the twentieth century with a regime of this character. With all peaceful means of change blocked by the military, the opposition parties and other organizations, including church groups, reached the conclusion that popular insurrection was the only means of obtaining freedom, genuine human rights and democracy for the people of El Salvador.
The United States once had a distinguished president by the name of Thomas Jefferson, and of all people in the world the people in the United States should understand that if an oligarchy controls a nation and tyrannical forces are in charge, the only alternative to such violence and tyranny organized by the state is violence in the hands of the people themselves. That is a regrettable truth, but a truth nonetheless.
The systematic and indiscriminate violence of the junta has continued, but to face this the Democratic Revolutionary Front was created. I want to say something about the front. The front was organized to co-ordinate the efforts of more than 40 organizations ranging from moderate priests and
professionals to social democrats, dissident Christian democrats and, yes, some Marxists. The leader of this movement is Manuel Ungo, now in exile in Mexico. Its program is not to set up an extremist, leftist state of an authoritarian kind; quite the contrary, its stated objective, reflecting its heterogeneous composition, is the creation of a political democracy with a mixed economy internationally non-aligned with any of the great powers. That surely is a commendable objective for an oppressed people.
At last count in El Salvador, at least 15,000 people have been killed, the majority victims of the armed forces and their semi-official death squads. There have been humane killings, although, of course, that is totally objectionable; but there have been indiscriminate killings on the part of the other side as well. That happens in a civil war. But there is no doubt at all as to what is the principal source and the principal agent of this conflict: it is the junta on the right. Mutilated corpses of the victims of the military regime remain in the streets of the capital. The most peaceful of people in the nation have been murdered. Monsignor Oscar Romero, archbishop of San Salvador, was gunned down right at the altar of his church last March because of his support for the legitimate aspirations of El Salvador's poor.
More recently, on October 4 the mutilated body of the spokeswoman for human rights, Maria Magdalena Henrigues, was found on the outskirts of San Salvador. One of the most gruesome incidents was the murder last May of more than 600 peasants by Salvadorean national guardsmen as the peasants attempted to flee across the border into Honduras.
The reality is that El Salvador is in a state of bloody civil war produced by a right-wing regime. This fact is obscured by the present United States government, which keeps portraying the present junta as representing moderation between the violent extremes of the left and right. The reality is quite different. The junta is part of the extreme right and is bereft of any popular support in the country. It lacks any shred of moral legitimacy and is thus inherently unstable. As William LeGrande and Carla Anne Robbins remarked in a recent issue of Foreign Affairs:
What Washington appears to be incapable of grasping is that in El Salvador, as in Nicaragua before it, the centrist forces which the United States perceives as its allies have joined with the very forces which the United States regards as its natural enemy-the radical left. The centrists are no longer in the centre .. . The recently unified left and centre left opposition includes everyone but the government and the far right.
That is the reality in El Salvador, whatever the current American state department would like everyone to believe. I regret to say that the people most zealously deploying the carefully contrived "moderate and reformist" image of the junta are supporters and advisers of the newly elected President of the United States, who announced in the presidential transition period that the Carter administration had been sponsoring social reform in El Salvador instead of "sticking to basics". As Alexander Cockburn in the current issue of Harpers magazine says, under these circumstances "-the basics are familiar enough: first find your dictator"-which is defined as firm leadership-"and then stick to him"-define
March 9, 1981

that as constancy to our allies-"however many people he kills."
Since President Reagan's election, military aid to the Salvadorean junta has been increasing on a regular basis. On March 3 it was reported that a total of 54 American military advisers had been sent to El Salvador and that $50 million in military aid has been pledged to the junta by the U.S. government. As a result of this military aid, including lethal weapons, the junta has been able to increase its capacity to kill peasants, dynamite organs of the Catholic church, and murder trade unionists. The military operations that the junta launches against the population, especially the rural population, have resulted in thousands of Salvadoreans abandoning their homes and becoming refugees. The churches have established seven refugee camps in the principal cities which house more than
3,000	displaced persons. In neighbouring countries, the number of refugees grows every day. In Honduras alone it is estimated there are more than 10,000 refugees. In Costa Rica there are 3,000. It has not been possible to calculate how many refugees are in Guatemala.
Instead of supporting such a regime, all democrats and certainly all democratic governments, including the Government of Canada, should join in their condemnation and mount pressure in the international community to bring peace and democracy to this troubled land.
Regrettably, and I mean that, because there has been a shift in U.S. policy, President Reagan's new policies extend well beyond El Salvador. The new American ambassador to the United Nations, Jean Kirkpatrick, recently explored a line of reasoning that has to disturb all of us. In the article entitled "Dictatorships and Double Standards", she presents arguments of the following kind in support of right-wing authoritarianism. First, she wrote:
Traditional autocrats... do not disturb the habitual rhythms of work and leisure, habitual patterns of family and personal relations. Because the miseries of traditional life are familiar, they are bearable to ordinary people-
She also writes, justifying a preference for right-wing authoritarianism over left-wing authoritarianism, that:
Although there is no instance of a revolutionary 'socialist' or communist society being democratized, right-wing autocracies do sometimes evolve into democracies-given time-
Regrettably, history does not accord with the ambassador's academic simplifications. In reality, the opposite has been the history of right-wing regimes throughout Latin America, as she should well know. Somoza firmly ruled for more than 45 years. El Salvador has had more than 50 years of military rule, as 1 have just sketched in.
What characterized these regimes and similar ones throughout Latin America is not a movement, as she suggests, toward democracy, but the systematic repression of all the ordinary people and civil libertarian forces in those countries that wanted to create democracy. That has been the real history, whatever the ambassador might say. The only equivalent to the new American apologetics for right-wing regimes in Latin
El Salvador
America is the kind of double-think attacks one finds now in Pravda on the solidarity movement in Poland. They are fully equivalent.
Those of us who believe in democracy must not get into the shallow game of "preferring" left-wing or right-wing repression. Repression is repression is repression, and I am disturbed that the new administration in the United States is about to wage a propagandistic battle in support of foreign policy steps designed to prop up, in a material way, right-wing regimes. The United States moves in support of the junta in El Salvador seem to me to be illustrations of a new, over-all foreign policy which completely abandons President Carter's commendable, if at times flawed, commitment to human rights.
A report in yesterday's New York Times is illustrative of this new direction in American foreign policy. The lead paragraph, not of an editorial but of a news item on about page 6, reads as follows:
The Reagan administration is moving rapidly to improve relations with South America's right-wing military regimes through invitations to military leaders from Chile, Brazil, and, in a few days, Argentina, for talks here.
What has Robert E. White, former U.S. ambassador to El Salvador, said about military support for such right-wing regimes? He said this:
To the extent that you emphasize a military solution in El Salvador, you are going to be buttressing one of the most out-of-control, violent, bloodthirsty groups of men in the world.
He warns that this kind of action is precisely the kind which will foster left-wing authoritarianism. He describes this new direction of the Reagan administration as a "disaster". Mr. White, the former U.S. ambassador in El Salvador, is right. We must do everything we can and so must the free world, to help the people of El Salvador; not prop up those who tyrannize them.
I want to turn immediately to the position of the Government of Canada, Mr. Speaker, and I will be brief. I could quote at considerable length the vacillating positions taken by the Government of Canada on this very important moral and practical issue of foreign policy. All I will say, however, is that the government has moved from acquiescence, on the one hand, to mild disapproval, on the other.
I should like to say on behalf of my colleagues that surely it is time for the Government of Canada to send a clear public message to the new administration in the United States which would consist of the following points. First, there should be no outside military intervention on the part of anyone in the terrible civil war that is going on in El Salvador. It should be left to the people in that troubled land to settle their own fate. Second, particularly the United States, as the world's first mass democracy, must not militarily prop up vicious regimes like that which operates in El Salvador. Finally, in a constructive mood, instead of acquiescing or being mildly critical, Canada should offer its services to join with other non-major powers like Mexico to play a mediating role in helping to bring both peace and democracy to El Salvador.
It is time to get off the fence. It is time to take some initiative to bring peace to this troubled land.

March 9, 1981
El Salvador

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for weeks now, indeed for months, our nightly newscasts and our newspapers have been filled with reports of the fighting, the brutality and the fear that characterizes El Salvador. A year ago, outsiders paid but little heed to this tiny Central American country. There were few who discussed it but many do so today, for today the world knows that El Salvador is a country in distress. It is a country whose people are locked into a class war, the great majority of whom are struggling for that kind of life which will offer them the opportunity for dignity and for hope. It is a country where fewer than 2 per cent of the population own more than half of the arable land, a country where the great bulk of the population live in abject poverty, their annual income a mere $600. It is a country which, as we know from history, has time and again expressed its desire for a democratic government, only to have those desires frustrated when elections were either disregarded or aborted.
These factors ought to remind us that El Salvador is not simply a pawn in the context of the United States and the Soviet Union. It reflects the problems of Third World countries, where people are seeking the twin objectives of economic development and political stability. As such, El Salvador should remind us that we are looking not just at a small country, but at an entire region of potential instability which could encompass not only Central America but the whole of the Caribbean.
All this makes more extraordinary the comments of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). In response to a question I posed to him last Tuesday, as recorded at page 7767 of Hansard, he said:
-I am not aware that we have any serious obligations in that part of the world, in Central America, which is not an area of traditional Canadian interest.
I would say to you, sir, that of course we have in that part of the world interests which are historic, geographic, economic and indeed moral. It is typical of this government to take such a narrow view of foreign policy. It leads to a failure to distinguish and analyse the consequences for Canada of situations like that in El Salvador. We ought to know by now that there are direct consequences for us. We need only recollect the human tragedy and the great difficulty caused by the flow of refugees from southeast Asia and the need for collective action to provide humanitarian relief to them.
Was southeast Asia also an area in which Canada had no interest? We have all the elements in El Salvador of a situation which could well produce a stream of refugees. It is estimated that already 60,000 people have fled that country to seek refuge in neighbouring states. I will be interested to see how the Secretary of State for External Affairs responds in the eventuality that an increasing number of El Salvadoreans become political refugees looking to countries such as Canada for assistance.
Then there is a broader sense in which Canada cannot remain indifferent to conflict in the western hemisphere. It has the potential to widen the rift between the United States and our European allies. It is clear, for example, that in the present situation West Germany is strongly opposed to the United States policy of injecting more arms into the conflict. I ask the minister, does the Canadian government have no interest in the potential that exists, as Vietnam did, to divide the alliance? It is obvious that we have both an interest and an obligation to explore any and all ways in which we can exercise a restraining influence, contrary to what the minister says.
I am already well on record as being opposed to military intervention by the United States in El Salvador or by any other power. The people of El Salvador are looking for a political solution to their problems, not a military one. Even members of the government of that country have said that there is already enough military equipment at the disposal of the junta. It is wrong for the United States to treat the problem as if it were solely in the context of East-West relations or to overdramatize the Soviet threat in El Salvador. There can be no doubt that some of its citizens are terrorists and insurgents and communist sympathizers, but their numbers are relatively few and their military might weak. We have only to look at the results of their recent military campaigns to see their very weakness.
We should also remember that there are extremists on the right who bear the responsibility for hundreds, perhaps thousands, of deaths and for human rights abuses. The present government, which lacks a popular basis of support and is becoming increasingly the captive of the right, had initially put into effect some social and economic reforms, but tragically all of these are now being held in abeyance. What is important for us to realize is that the great majority of the people in El Salvador lie between the extremes of right and left. Motivated to improve their conditions, they have found a response to their efforts in the support and encouragement they have received from church groups of all denominations, particularly Catholic bishops, and from non-governmental organizations from many countries.
The majority of the population in El Salvador is not looking for arms but for aid to reach its objectives. The great fear I have is that if additional military equipment and force of arms are used against them by a government which lacks credibility, they could be pushed further and further to extremes. The civil war could escalate rapidly if the right and the left factions were further armed one against the other. In that case, the strength of the large majority of people would be lost and that, above all, is what we must seek to avoid.
The government should make it plain that it believes the United States should do nothing to aggravate the situation, and neither should any other country. Until a short time ago, I would have thought the Liberal government more or less shared these views, even though the Secretary of State for External Affairs had indicated his unwillingness, as he put it, "to lead a public crusade" against United States military involvement in El Salvador.
March 9, 1981

Earlier statements and actions had indicated, so I thought, Canada's strong backing for non-interference. For example, a joint communique of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Brazilian foreign minister on October 1, 1980, stated:
The two ministers exchanged views about the current situation in Latin America and the Caribbean . . . They expressed the hope that the countries concerned would be able to overcome their difficulties without foreign interference and in accordance with the wishes of their peoples.
Again, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will recall meeting with the Mexican foreign minister. They issued a communique on January 9, 1981 which stated:
The two foreign ministers ... expressed the hope that the existing conflicts in Central America will be resolved by means of the free expression of the will of the respective peoples and without foreign interference.
I would draw the minister's attention once more to the vote taken on the resolution at the United Nations on December 15, 1980, a resolution for which Canada voted. That resolution reads:
Considering that the supply of arms and other military assistance will serve to aggravate the situation in that country, the General Assembly calls upon governments to refrain from the supply of arms and other military assistance in the current circumstances.
What we voted for at the United Nations was "to refrain from the supply of arms and other military assistance in the current circumstances". What, then, are we to make of the comment by the minister, after consultation with officials of the Reagan administration-a comment he has refused to deny-that:
I would certainly not condemn any decision the United States takes to send offensive arms ... the United States can count on our quiet acquiescence-
Or quiescence, as he later corrected. His previous so-called commitment to non-intervention makes all the more appalling the minister's declaration on February 4. I find it very difficult to understand, in light of the previous statements by the minister when he met with foreign ministers from Brazil, Venezuela and Mexico and when he instructed the delegation at the United Nations to vote for non-interference, that he would make the statement he did on February 4, that he would not condemn any decision the United States takes to send weapons to El Salvador. I believe that is wrong, as I believe it is wrong for any nation to send arms to El Salvador.
Not only does it repudiate Canada's approach at the United Nations, not only does it repudiate the expressed views of the Canadian government taken jointly with the governments of Mexico, Brazil and Venezuela, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs' attitude of quiet acquiescence demonstrates that he is incapable of making independent judgments, based on Canada's interest, when faced by American foreign policy-makers.
A foreign minister must be able to distinguish between requests for solidarity that are inevitable and those that are unnecessary. As Secretary of State for External Affairs at the time, 1 sought to lend full support to the Carter administration in response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. I was
El Salvador
convinced that we ought to condemn that invasion. In fact, although the government of which 1 was a part was much criticized by the official opposition in Ottawa at that time, we sought positive ways in which to communicate to the Soviets our determined opposition to their behaviour. That behaviour threatened detente and made a general conflict more likely, and I would say that in the case of Poland we have a similar need to impress on the Soviets our unshakeable opposition to any military intervention. 1 wish the minister would be stronger in his statements to this effect.
But a foreign minister must be able to distinguish between Afghanistan and El Salvador. Nothing that has been said here this afternoon removes the minister's statement of February 4 from the record, or explains his failure to address the underlying issues.
What can Canada do? I ask that because 1 think it is important that we not merely raise criticisms but that we try to offer constructive suggestions to help resolve the increasing conflict in El Salvador. In the short term, it may be possible for this country to contribute to the improvement of the situation by engaging in extensive consultation with El Salvador's neighbouring states to obtain their views on the present situation, and to determine whether there is the possibility of an international role to insulate El Salvador from external interference.
Second, the Canadian government should explore the possibility of international action through the United Nations or another appropriate international body. The purpose would be to establish the degree of outside intervention in El Salvador and to monitor the situation while the conflict continues. Such an international body could have a stabilizing effect and be the start of a process leading to a political settlement not only in that troubled country, but in that very troubled part of the world. In exploring this possibility, we might be able to associate ourselves with such countries as Brazil, Venezuela, Mexico and West Germany, all of which have been willing to provide good offices to help stabilize the situation.
These are the short-run possibilities. In the long run what we must realize is that these conflicts will never be resolved as long as the underlying causes are ignored. It is senseless for the government, through the minister, to say that we have no interest in El Salvador while, on the other hand, it prides itself on promoting the North-South dialogue. Until we are willing to treat the basic issues of health, nutrition, housing, education and employment, we will continue to be faced with the tensions that today beset El Salvador and elsewhere in Central America.
There is a strong case for increasing Canadian aid both to Central America and to the Caribbean since these are areas which will most affect us if they are to become more and more a region of conflict and instability. One of my major interests as minister was to focus the attention of my department on the Caribbean and Central America, an interest the present minister does not appear to share.
For these reasons, I would like to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) convey to President Reagan our disappoint-

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
ment that the United States does not intend to place a high priority on foreign aid and the North-South dialogue. He should assure the President that Canada is willing to play its part and more, but that we look for greater commitment and leadership on this critical issue from the United States, which is, after all, the wealthiest and most powerful state.
In all of this we should remember that the people of El Salvador have an absolute right to determine their own future without foreign intervention. Our task is to help create the circumstances in which the parties in El Salvador can continue their own negotiations. What we can hope for in that process is for a government that will represent the will of the people of El Salvador.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the fundamental problem with the motion before the House today is that its drafters are people with an obsession with black and white, and a permanent feature of their obsession is obviously that black is always to be presumptively deemed the colour of the American side and white that of the fighting left.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: You didn't listen to my speech.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
I am speaking about the motion. The hon. gentleman may have tried in his speech to disguise the heart of his motion, but his motion is in exactly the terms I am describing. In my view, a debate conducted on the premises of today's motion would be more suitable for a high school auditorium than for this distinguished chamber.
The motion identifies the government of El Salvador as a repressive regime "fighting those who wish to establish a democratic government". Opinions may perhaps differ as to the character of the regime but not as to the character and motivations of those fighting against it. As Robert E. White, the former U.S. ambassador to El Salvador, quoted fulsomely by the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), said in a colloquy, sponsored by members of the Congress for Peace Through Law on February 26, which was printed by the New York Times yesterday:
The ultimate enemy of western civilization and of the U.S. in El Salvador is a Marxist-Leninist group dedicated to the overthrow of the government by force, and the elimination of all U.S. influence from that region.
Another participant in the colloquium put it this way:
Even though the political leaders of the left, like Guillermo Ungo, have impeccable democratic credentials, the men with the guns-according to Mr. White-are committed Marxist-Leninists.
According to the simplistic pieties of this motion, however, the men with the guns are "those who wish to establish a democratic government".
It would appear that the Leader of the New Democratic Party does not wish to condemn the use of these guns or the supply of such guns to the revolutionary forces in El Salvador which were being supplied months before the United States began to supply arms there. On the contrary, he seems to condone it or perhaps even commend it because he argued in
the House on March 2 that the left-wing forces are somehow morally justified in military action against the government of El Salvador.
