speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased the hon. gentleman takes that position today but he implied something else in the House on March 2, and that is what I was quoting.
We have our differences with the United States on El Salvador and we are prepared to express them, but our differences are not over rejecting the violence, whether from the Marxist-Leninist left or from the extreme right, or over halting the importation of huge quantities of arms from Cuba and other communist countries through Nicaragua into El Salvador. Our differences are principally with respect to the provision of American military assistance to the government of El Salvador, which we believe is neither desirable nor necessary.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
I am obviously getting to those hon. members, Mr. Speaker. They obviously do not like hearing the truth.
We have expressed our disagreement with the American government on this point both privately and publicly, but we believe in doing so in terms which are appropriate to the cause and not wildly inflated because of some paranoia of the left. President Reagan has insisted that sending American troops to El Salvador is "not in our reckoning at all". Secretary of State Haig has warned right-wing extremists in El Salvador that a rightist coup would have serious consequences to the continuation of U.S. aid.
In light of the full circumstances, therefore, as we see them, we are prepared to contest the U.S. policy of military aid but not to protest it; we are prepared to pronounce on it but not to denounce it; we are prepared to criticize it but not to condemn it. As the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has said, one must distinguish between El Salvador and Afghanistan. It is unfortunate she was unable to make that distinction and would denounce this action of the U.S. in terms of the kind which she and others used to describe Soviet
March 9, 1981

action in Afghanistan. In other words, we believe in seeing the situation in El Salvador as it is and also in describing it as it is, not as idees fixes might describe it.
In turning to a fuller exposition of the position of the Canadian government, it might be useful if I were first to provide the government's perspective of the nature of change affecting Central America as a whole and the extent of Canada's ties, capabilities, and interests with this part of the world before dealing with El Salvador in detail.
The countries of Central America are undergoing a difficult process of change from traditional regimes to new species of political, social and economic organizations. In certain states change is being accompanied by increasing violence and instability.
It is interesting that those over there on the left suggest I should not lecture them. We have just been subjected to another lecture from that side, so why should we not have our say over here?
Economically, the impact of external influences, in particular oil price rises, increased costs for other imports, fluctuating prices for principal export commodities and the reduction in economic activity in industrialized countries have slowed economic growth throughout Central America in recent years. Internal political and security problems are now affecting economic performance. In Costa Rica, the only state in the region with a long-standing tradition of democracy, the rising costs of social services have led to severe fiscal constraints. The governments of other Central American states, dominated by right-wing military dictators throughout most of their history, neglected the social sector until recently and have not had to face the same economic problem.
These states are now paying dearly for this neglect. Unresolved social problems are at the heart of pressures for political change and constitute the single most important cause of regional instability. It is no coincidence that the highest levels of instability in Latin America are to be found in Central America where general standards of health care, nutrition and literacy are among the lowest in the hemisphere. It is likewise no coincidence that hemispheric instability is centred in the region which has the highest rate of population growth in Latin America, with a population expected to grow from its present level of 20 million to 40 million by the year 2000.
While conditions differ among states, unequal income distribution, high rates of population growth, unemployment and unresolved agrarian problems are the most serious socioeconomic problems throughout Central America. The income distribution problem is probably the most important. Gulfs between "haves" and "have nots" have widened in recent years as the increase in wealth derived from growing national economies has not been passed on to the populations who have suffered losses in real income through inflation. The problem in Central America is one of growing expectations as populations seek to obtain a larger share of the benefits of economic growth.
El Salvador
This lack of government attention to basic human needs has in large part generated the internal pressures for change in El Salvador and Guatemala and was the major stimulus behind the overthrow of the Somoza government. Attention to the social needs of populations in Honduras and in Panama has led to greater stability in these states.
Politically, as recently as two years ago, all states of the area except Costa Rica were governed by military dictatorships allied to conservative oligarchies. Since that time dramatic changes have occurred in those states which formerly opposed even moderate change. In Nicaragua, popular discontent developed into a struggle led by the Sandinistas supported from abroad and resulted in the downfall of Somoza.
Turning to human rights, with some exceptions a tradition of respect for human rights, whether political, social or economic, has never existed in Central America. On the contrary, political violence, both in support of the traditional power structure and perpetuated against its representatives, has been a constant of regional political life for decades.
New leaders are emerging in both the military and economic establishments of all countries who recognize the need to modernize societies, to steer their states through a period of complex transition and to effect social and political justice. They are opposed by representatives of the traditional power structure and are often victims of right and left-wing extremists-from the former, the right-wing extremists, for betraying their origins, and from the latter, the left-wing extremists, for threatening to remove the basis for revolutionary change. In both El Salvador and Guatemala, the actions of both left and right have eliminated many leading moderates. In Nicaragua, gross violations of human rights did not occur following the overthrow of Somoza but limitations have been placed on press freedoms and elections have been postponed until 1985.
What is the nature of Canada's involvement in the region in these circumstances? Central America, unlike the neighbouring Commonwealth Caribbean, has not been the focus of traditional Canadian interest and bilateral political contacts have been infrequent. Canadians have had little in common with the ruling oligarchies and have regarded with repugnance the violence and widespread violations of human rights which have characterized the Central American political scene.
Commercial and economic development ties have been and will remain of some importance. Economically, Canadian investment in Central America is of significance, totalling about $300 million for the region. However, over $250 million of this investment is concentrated in one industry, nickel extraction, and in one country, Guatemala. Investors are now being discouraged by political uncertainty. Central America also constitutes an important market for Canadian businessmen, with annual exports totalling over $100 million, much of which is labour-intensive manufactured goods.
In development assistance terms, despite the absence of close political ties, Canada has recognized the pressing needs of the region and has been a leading aid donor in Central

March 9, i 98 i
El Salvador
America, providing more than $60 million in bilateral aid since 1972. In terms of concentration, Honduras and El Salvador, as the poorest of the area, have received the largest portion of the funding.
El Salvador and Honduras are program countries. Guatemala is a project country, and Costa Rica and Nicaragua are eligible for mission administered funds only. Cabinet has agreed that Nicaragua will become a project country effective April of this year. At the present time, the assistance to Guatemala which started in the wake of the 1976 earthquake is being allowed to run out, given the growing levels of violence in that country, and planning for new projects has been suspended in El Salvador as a consequence of the civil war.
What does this mean in terms of Canadian policy toward the area? In contrast to the neighbouring Commonwealth Caribbean, where Canada has long been regarded as a major outside power, Canada has no special expertise or capability in Central American affairs and is not as well placed as regional states, such as Venezuela or Mexico, to exert a positive influence on the evolution of the area. Canada's interests, while important and growing, are likewise not of the same order of importance as our interests elsewhere in Latin America, such as in Mexico, Venezuela and Brazil. While naturally sharing the concern of the international community, we therefore have no more obligation than other states in taking a leading role in resolving the conflict.
Turning now to deal specifically with El Salvador, Canada has never had major bilateral ties with that country; and has no resident ambassador there. However, in recent years we have been involved in providing development assistance in recognition of the pressing economic needs of its population.
The basic problems of El Salvador, which has the highest population density and the lowest per capita income of any country in Central America, relate to the critical need of the people of that country for opportunities of economic development and social justice which have been denied them for many decades by a series of authoritarian governments.
Canada, like many other countries, welcomed the overthrow of the dictatorial regime of general Carlos Romero in 1979 and its replacement by the government of progressive civilian and military leaders. This government adopted a number of social and economic measures which it believed would bring about needed social reforms. For example, it nationalized the banks and foreign trade. It also took initial steps to introduce a much needed land reform and adopted other measures in an attempt to provide a government which would be more attentive to the political, social and economic needs and aspirations of the population.
The new civilian-military junta was not very successful in accomplishing its worth-while objectives. It encountered increasing opposition from extremist right-wing elements both within the government security forces and outside the government, often financed by expatriate supporters of the previous regime who objected to the reform program, and also from left-wing forces who felt either that the reform movement was
not moving forward fast enough or who saw it as diminishing their own political influence. During the course of 1980 both these right-wing and left-wing opponents of the civilian-military junta government resorted to increasing intimidation and attacks on the government. They perpetrated an escalating number of murders, assassinations, tortures and other atrocities which have shocked the conscience of the world.
In December, 1980 the civilian-military junta underwent an internal reorganization designed to enable it to proceed more successfully with its political and social objectives and Mr. Jose Napoleon Duarte, a respected Christian democrat, was made president. In 1972, in one of the few honest elections in El Salvador, Mr. Duarte emerged as victor but was prevented from taking power by a military coup. He is widely believed to be the best person to lead a reformist government at the present time. President Duarte has pledged to turn over 40 per cent of the land to small land owners, to proceed with other social reforms, to hold free elections in 1982-three years earlier, I might add, than the leftist regime in Nicaragua-and to grant an amnesty to left-wing guerrillas. President Duarte's government has dismissed a number of military officers accused of human rights abuses and has very recently ordered the arrest of a notorious right-wing retired major who has alledgedly been advocating a right-wing military coup. Unfortunately President Duarte's government has experienced the same attacks from the left and the right, with the result that the human tragedy and loss of lives in El Salvador continues unabated.
When considering the current situation in El Salvador, it is important to put developments into the historical context which I previously outlined and to remember that, despite its failings and weaknesses, it is still the legal government of El Salvador and is recognized as such in the United Nations by Canada and by all other governments. While there are conflicting views held about the ability of the Duarte government to achieve its objectives of political, social and economic reform, we consider, as do many other governments in western Europe and in Latin America, that in the present circumstances it may nevertheless still be the most feasible channel through which the people of El Salvador can achieve democratic solutions to their political, economic and social problems if its extremist opponents on the left and the right can be brought under control.
The consistent position of the Government of Canada has been to deplore the senseless violence in El Salvador and to urge that the people of El Salvador be allowed to settle their political and economic difficulties peacefully and democratically without outside interference. These sentiments were shared by other governments and were endorsed in the communiques I mentioned in the House on March 2, which the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has paid me the courtesy of reading this afternoon. That is exactly our policy.
In late 1980 and early 1981, the level of violence in El Salvador continued to escalate and the revolutionary forces mounted increasingly concentrated armed attacks on the government with the apparent intention of overthrowing it by
March 9, 1981

armed force. Prior to this time the government of the United States had supplied the government of El Salvador with a modest amount of non-lethal military equipment, such as communications equipment, uniforms, etc. However, when it became apparent that the revolutionary forces had obtained substantial quantities of arms, many of them of a sophisticated nature, and were bent on the overthrow of the legitimate government, the outgoing Carter administration authorized the supply of lethal military equipment to enable the government of El Salvador to deal with the threat to overthrow it.
On January 26, 1981, I met in Ottawa with two representatives of the revolutionary side who told me that their arms were acquired by purchase on the international arms black market with funds which had been acquired by bank robberies and kidnapping of businessmen and foreign diplomats, including the ambassador of South Africa who was subsequently murdered by his captors. In this context it is worth noting that these revolutionary forces have been responsible for 28 assaults on foreign embassies in the last two years, as well as armed attacks on the Salvadorian foreign ministry and other government buildings. The Swiss charge d'affaires was killed in 1979; the French ambassador was kidnapped within hours of his arrival in San Salvador and was held for 30 days; the Costa Rican embassy has been occupied three times in the past year and a half. The record and conduct of extremist right-wing elements, both within and without the government security forces, is equally bad. They are believed to be responsible for the assassination of Archbishop Romero, just a year ago this month, and the brutal murders of priests, Salvadorian politicians and American churchwomen.
Subsequently the United States government published a white paper on February 23, 1981 indicating that the United States had obtained incontrovertible evidence that massive amounts of weapons and military equipment of western origin, presumably to disguise their source-some of which have been specifically identified as being U.S. weapons left behind in Vietnam-had been provided to the revolutionary forces in El Salvador by a number of socialist bloc countries and funnelled through Nicaragua, with the apparent co-operation of some officials of the Nicaraguan government. We have no reason to doubt this evidence, which is also accepted as valid by many other governments.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: And no reason to accept it, either.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
The current political and military situation in El Salvador is obviously highly fluid and we are not in a position to make assessments on the basis of first-hand information. However, our policy is not confused. On the contrary, it has been clear, concise and consistent. Throughout this period it has been the Canadian government's policy not to supply arms to either side in El Salvador or to any other country in Central America. I might say that there was a grievous error recently in the Toronto Globe and Mail in which it stated to the contrary. The information was obtained as a result of a reporter reading the wrong column in a series
El Salvador
of statistics, but the newspaper has never bothered to correct the record. The policy has thus been consistently implemented, and press reports to the contrary are quite inaccurate.
We do not believe that the problems of El Salvador can be resolved by military measures. We urge all other governments to follow the same policy and refrain from supplying offensive weapons, the use of which only causes increased violence and suffering for the people of El Salvador. We strongly support the traditional principle of international law, which is one of opposition to any interference from the outside in another country's domestic affairs.
We also believe that the problems of El Salvador can be solved only through political discussion and negotiation by the Salvadorian parties directly concerned. 1 explained this to the representatives of the revolutionary forces when 1 met with them in January. I also explained it to Secretary Haig in Washington. I have explained it to the House, and I have explained it many times to the Canadian news media. It will serve no useful purpose to engage in public denunciations. 1 can assure the House that we will continue to make our views in this regard known in bilateral contacts with the United States and in the appropriate multilateral fora, as we have done in the past, as and when appropriate.
We fully share the sentiments of hon. members with respect to the killings, atrocities and abuses of human rights in El Salvador and, like all Canadians, we deplore them. Bilaterally, we have made frequent representations to the government of El Salvador. Multilaterally, we have been among the most active of all states in fora such as the OAS and the United Nations in seeking to mobilize international opinion in favour of a greater respect for human rights in the Salvadorian conflict. During the current session of the UN Human Rights Commission we are actively working for a constructive resolution which will call for a restoration of respect for human rights and an end to all arms supplies to all parties in El Salvador.
As for the future, we believe that there is an urgent need for a political settlement which will enable the moderate democratic elements in the government of El Salvador and in the revolutionary forces to coalesce. Canada welcomes the first signs of a willingness to negotiate on the part of the government. The president of El Salvador, Mr. Duarte, has recently indicated that his government is prepared to have a dialogue with the revolutionary forces, and it is now up to those forces to respond. We have no illusions that the process will be easy, since the more extreme elements on both sides will resist making the concessions necessary for a lasting solution. In the interim, the revolutionary forces should cease undermining the efforts of the government to introduce its reform package, and both sides should take immediate steps to stamp out mindless violence.
Having made those points, it should be remembered that historically Canada has not had strong or important links with El Salvador. It is a country near our part of the world but hardly a neighbour. However, the human tragedy of El Salvador has engaged the attention of all countries.

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
In this situation, what are our responsibilities? The first is to try to inform ourselves so that when we discuss these issues we at least do so knowledgeably. Even this is not easy. Much of our information is indirect and partial. It is refracted through the prisms of particular points of view before it reaches us. Views conflict and there is even conflict about matters of fact.
In the circumstances, the views of countries near El Salvador or with more important interests in El Salvador than Canada are more important to us. We note that some of these countries, whose views we respect, have taken a stand close to our own. There has yet been no initiative to refer the situation in El Salvador to the United Nations, nor is it being dealt with in the OAS. A number of countries have said, as we have, that the flow of arms from whatever source should cease, and that political and economic solutions to El Salvador's problems should be sought. But no government-not Mexico, Venezuela or the Federal Republic of Germany-contrary to the words of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, has yet gone beyond this to launch a political initiative in order to bring an end to the internal strife with the aid of some outside mediator. Therefore, it hardly seems prudent for Canada to put itself in such a role, if that is what the opposition is advocating.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Indeed, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, in her capacity as secretary of state for external affairs, came to the same conclusion concerning Nicaragua as I have with respect to El Salvador.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: No, indeed I did not. We sent aid.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
I recall her words on the radio program "As It Happens" on July 6, 1979:
-we are not in a position to carry out any special relations with Nicaragua ... I am not advocating that Canada jump in with any kind of a force or with any kind of a heavy hand to try to straighten out an internal, very difficult problem in Nicaragua, nor would I either in Nicaragua or in other countries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: I certainly was not advocating force.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
In short, we have no more responsibility in the matter than any other sovereign state and, in practice, a good deal less knowledge and standing in relation to the problems of El Salvador than a number of other countries. Any sensible Canadian policy has to take these limitations into account. Sheer outpourings of moral indignation are not much help. They may ease the conscience but they do not advance the solution.
I think it is clear that there is no substantial ground whatsoever for this House to support this motion. I urge members to see the motion for what it is, namely, a calculated attempt to create tension between the Government of Canada and the government of the United States which will not add one iota of practical assistance to the real sufferers in this issue, namely, the people of El Salvador.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate as a friend of the United States and, more important, as a friend of the millions upon millions of people throughout the world today whose economic and social rights are being grossly violated. I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) will not accuse me of moral outpourings of rage when I add to the words already spoken on the floor this afternoon about the real human tragedy that is at the heart of this motion.
I said I was a friend of the United States. I lived in the United States, Mr. Speaker, for ten years; indeed, three of my children were born in that country. I have travelled extensively through it and I feel that I have had the opportunity of understanding a great people. It is precisely because of that understanding and that friendship that I have for the United States that I am so opposed to continued American military involvement in El Salvador.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
But I say to the movers of the motion that it is a defective motion since it merely addresses itself to the question of the United States abstaining from or getting out of military involvement in El Salvador. It does not go on to make positive statements or recommendations, or even express a positive idea of what should be done in El Salvador in order to speak to the reasons why the Americans feel that they must prop up a regime for which the real contempt of this House should be expressed. I hope that in the few moments I have I will indicate a much more positive role for the United States to play in El Salvador and in that larger community of interest, the developing countries today, where 800 million people are grievously suffering from a lack of basic human needs.
El Salvador has suddenly been catapulted into international prominence. Do hon. members think the picture I have in my hand, which illustrates an article in the New York Times Sunday magazine entitled "The Agony of El Salvador", in which the corpses of two women are shown with their hands tied behind their backs, is the work of people who care about the suffering inside El Salvador? The residue of the famous 14 families of El Salvador has become its wealthy landowners. Listen to the New York Times description of this country:
And some 60 per cent of El Salvador's population is rural-
We already know there are five million people in that country, which is smaller in size than Vancouver Island.
-living in isolated valleys or mountain hamlets. Wooden-yoked oxen draw carts that ride on solid wooden wheels. Hundreds of thousands of peasants live in hovels made of packed mud; naked children with swollen bellies and open sores wander among the grunting pigs, garbage and flies. Their mothers and sisters trudge for an hour or more to the nearest well for water, carried in gourd-shaped plastic containers balanced on their heads.
A distinguished Canadian journalist, Hugh McCullum, the editor of the United Church Observer, went to El Salvador. After recounting the statistics of low caloric intake, high infant mortality and high percentages of malnutrition and illiteracy, Mr. McCullum says this:
March 9, 1981

The pattern is brutal exploitation, in which wealthy landowners have branched into industry and banking, even though they have now left the country with their profits, while the soldiers and police are used to ensure a steady supply of land, and a cheap and docile labour force.
That is at the heart of the situation in El Salvador and has led to a radicalization of the poor. When they became radicalized and aggressive, it was too much for the regime known as the juntas. It claims to have some validity since Duarte himself was elected in 1972. Irrespective of the legitimacy of the regime, it has had to react against this gradual coming together of the poor, who are helped by some of their own leaders. They rebel against 2 per cent of the people of the country owning 60 per cent of the land and against the conditions of misery into which their children are born.
The internal reforms which have been brought to El Salvador by the Duarte regime have clearly not lasted because they were not undertaken with conviction. The attempt to nationalize the banks and the sugar cane industry has fizzled out. Some people in El Salvador have been helped to improve themselves, but the reform never became a sign of hope to the people in El Salvador because it was immediately met by a wave of repression, goon squads employed by the wealthy and a paramilitary organization of the government.
Do hon. members think that it was the landless people who live in misery who shot Archbishop Romero while he was saying mass in his own cathedral in San Salvador, or who murdered nine priests, or who brutally slayed four American missionaries? Those killings can be laid at the door of the extreme right, the fanatics who want to stop any social reform which would benefit the wide masses of the people in El Salvador.
The Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops has undertaken an in-depth survey and study of El Salvador, and I quote two major findings:
The vast majority of the victims of repression come from the poorer sectors, and proof can be established that they were murdered either by extreme right commandos or by the military;-
That is the first of the major findings. The second is this:
The junta systematically persecutes all progressive organizations claiming to do so in order to protect its centrist position against the extreme left. Yet, it does nothing to stop the actions of the paramilitary extreme right, let alone uncovering the real leaders behind them.
Along comes Ambassador White, relieved of his ambassadorial post representing the United States in El Salvador by the new Reagan administration, who says the policy of the American government to use military intervention to shore up this regime which is largely responsible for a wave of killings-which now total 13,194 over the past couple of years-is a policy of madness. Moreover, he says that these so-called leftist forces are only about 2,000, that there is not the slightest possibility that they could upset the ruling government and, in fact, that the ruling government had this situation well in hand.
Why, then, do we see the new American government pouring funds into, and augmenting its military advisers-now up to about 50-in a country in which there is no real threat that the government will be overthrown? Of course, we know that
El Salvador
the reason is to stop communist advance in Central America. I applaud a stopping of the communist advance anywhere in the world, but to try to stop the communist advance by loading the problem on to the backs and shoulders of the poor in El Salvador is not the answer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Ambassador White said during his debate with Ambassador Kirkpatrick, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, which took place last week:
The important thing to realize is that this present government stopped the leftists cold, without receiving one rifle from the United States. Now is not the time to emphasize military assistance. Now is the time-when the leftists have been defeated-to emphasize a political solution.
To the extent that you emphasize a military solution in El Salvador, you are going to be buttressing one of the most out-of-control, violent, bloodthirsty groups of men in the world. They have killed-at a minimum-5,000 or 6,000 kids, just on the mere suspicion that they were involved with the leftists.
Archbishop Hickey, testifying before a House subcommittee last week and speaking for the American Catholic bishops as well as from his own experience in El Salvador, said that the situation there "is not principally a matter of guns, but of justice." He said that American bishops oppose military aid to El Salvador and find it "particularly ominous" that military advisers are being sent. He also said:
It is risky to the point of being reckless. It confirms the worst suspicions of Latin Americans that we are preparing for an invasion of El Salvador.
Again, referring to Pope John Paul's comments in the Philippines about human rights for workers in the course of his most recent journey, Archbishop Hickey said:
I can assure you that if some of those things that were said by the Holy Father were said in El Salvador by the simple catechists, by the local parish priests, that person would be in danger of his life.
In the issue of March 2, The Christian Science Monitor carried an article by Geoffrey Godsell who put his finger on the core of the situation. The lead paragraph reads as follows:
The Reagan administration has clearly chosen El Salvador as the best of the options available to send a signal to-and even test-the Soviet Union.
Today we find ourselves debating this issue. I believe that it is absolutely essential for the United States to hear from its friends around the world. As the closest neighbour, and I venture to say the closest friend, I believe that Canada ought to be able to speak frankly to the Reagan administration and I hope that the Canadian government will do so when President Reagan is here. I believe that we must be much more forthright than we have been in the past and that we ought to accompany our criticism of the present involvement in El Salvador with a plea to the United States that it is absolutely essential that it play a leading role in acting to redress the great conditions of misery that are producing the El Salvadors of the world. El Salvador will not be alone because 800 million people live in the same kind of conditions as are found there.
I think we must encourage the United States to resume the role it has played over the years. If we look back at the Marshall Plan we remember that, following the end of the

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
hostilities of World War II, the United States was very concerned that western Europe should not fall into the hands of the communists. In order to help western Europe, it sent over massive amounts of economic and social development aid. Those are the signals that the American government ought to be sending today.
In the North-South dialogue the United States has already given early signals that it is very cool to the issue and shows a lack of any element of concern. An illustration of that was the cutback in its foreign aid budget. The United States must be encouraged by Canada and others to play a leading role in the North-South Summit. If it indicates that it is not interested in attending the North-South Summit, I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to others who play a leading role that the United States should be encouraged to attend; indeed, I say that pressure should be mounted to hold the summit in Mexico irrespective of the position or the United States.
Finally I come to the position of Canada. I listened carefully today to the Secretary of State for External Affairs as he recounted our involvement through our international development program in Central America. Our financial involvement in El Salvador and Nicaragua is minimal relative to the total CIDA budget. As host to the economic summit which will deal with the North-South question, I find it strange, when speaking to the problem of poverty in the world, that we should do so little about El Salvador. Even today I believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not spoken as forthrightly as increasing numbers of Canadians would like our government to speak. They want it to say clearly that it opposes intervention by any government in El Salvador, that it opposes the sale of arms, the transfer of arms or gun-running by anybody. We believe that a political solution can and should be worked out through the United Nations.
The minister said that we would not take an initiative beyond that which our major partners in the west would take. Why not? Why cannot Canada raise its voice at the United Nations? Why cannot we propose an international commission for El Salvador? Why cannot we emphasize human rights, indivisible? Why cannot we emphasize development throughout the developing world? Why cannot we emphasize that this country will pay special attention to those who are most oppressed, those who live in regimes that are beneath contempt in their treatment of human life?
May I close by saying that if we are truly serious about fighting communism-and the United States is using this as its excuse-then I think we have to emphasize that the only way to make our world a safe, secure and stable place is to emphasize social reform and justice for the downtrodden people of the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear from the way the motion before us is worded that it requires us to think about two aspects of the role that Canada should play in relation to what has been happening in El Salvador, and at the same time, to make an attempt to understand what is going on in that part of the world.
It seems to me that it is important for those of us in this House and elsewhere who are interested in what is happening in Central America these days to understand the nature and the dynamics of the forces operating in that part of the World. We must also endeavour to make the people in Washington understand what is involved here, in their own best interests. That may sound presumptuous, put in those terms, but I am convinced that it is essential to make an extra effort at understanding.
Before I develop that thought, Mr. Speaker, I should like to address myself to that part of the motion that deals with civil and human rights and put on the record, very briefly, Canada's role so far in relation to El Salvador.
March 9, 1981

First, it can be said that our concern about the situation in El Salvador predates the present controversy. We have been pursuing all the avenues available to us in the human rights field. We supported the resolution of concern at the Copenhagen international conference last summer. We have brought the full measure of our concern at the violence and human rights abuses in El Salvador to the attention of its government. At the present time, Canada is working with other delegations in Geneva to ensure that the Human Rights Commission will adopt a resolution calling for an end to the violence and violations of human rights by all elements in El Salvador and for an end to the supply of armaments to all parties in that country. The resolution calls for a peaceful political solution to the problems in El Salvador and for the appointment of a special rapporteur to inquire into the situation.
Next, Canada is responding to the plight of the people in El Salvador who have fled their country. The United Nations refugee commission is assisting those in asylum in the general region, and Canada has recently increased its contribution to the regular budget from $2.5 million to $4 million for such purposes. Canada has also responded with a $250,000 contribution, which represents roughly 10 per cent of the Red Cross current appeal for assistance to El Salvadorians.
No matter what steps we take to help the plight of people affected, and no matter what short-term recommendations we may be able to put forward this afternoon in this House, one fact remains clear. What is developing in El Salvador cannot be looked upon in isolation from a trend in other parts of the world where there is a concentration of power in the hands of governments which grasp power for themselves through nondemocratic means, and where governments have failed over the decades, maybe over the centuries, to achieve the level of social justice that we have in our western democracies.
The situation under debate here this afternoon in the long run could be another Cuba, if the extreme government in power now in El Salvador were to be replaced in the future by another extremist government of a different stripe. Already in Nicaragua we talk about a second Cuba. It could well be that other countries in Central and Latin America are destined to follow the fate of Cuba. It was only two or three decades ago when the United States witnessed, I suppose to its own dismay, the replacement in Cuba of a government headed by Batista with that of Castro. It would be desirable that we make an effprt to understand why and how it happened. I can understand the fears and the concerns of the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), but nevertheless I urge him as I would urge anyone to attempt to understand why countries develop and accept totalitarian regimes.
We cannot look at El Salvador in the context of what has happened just in the last few months. We have to ask ourselves why El Salvador is going through its present troubles. Is El Salvador facing a situation whereby the neglect of basic reforms, such as social reform, redistribution of wealth, land reform and other forms of basic human justice, get overlooked
El Salvador
for such a long period of time that sooner or later people do catch up with their governments?
It is becoming fairly evident in a number of countries that the populations are beginning to disagree with established oligarchies of one stripe or the other which came to power through some exercise, of violence, probably with the support of some power abroad. It could well be that the entire Central American region, not just El Salvador, is in danger. If that were the case, then the consequences could be serious. This troubled situation may even occur as far north as the location of Mexico's oil reserves. Will we then be able to justify our concern only within the confines of the El Salvadorian situation? Obviously we cannot do that.
It seems to me that we have a gigantic task before us. We have to explain to our American friends how the situation in El Salvador evolved. We must explain that beyond considerations of power there are considerations of a social nature which have to be taken into account. The propping up of one government, as the experience of Cuba teaches, is not sufficient in the long run to ensure that a government will remain in power. The lesson which the West must have learned from the Cuban experience is one which is as valid today as it was 25 years ago. We cannot look at these events in isolation. They cannot be separated from the inadequacies of social reforms, the redistribution of wealth, the absence of the democratic means of change and the absence of democratic parties as we know them. So long as these countries are looked upon as areas for security not as an area where the security of one nation is at stake-because there are also basic fundamental social shortcomings, to put it mildly-we will not be dealing with the roots of the problem. We may be running the risk of dealing only with the symptoms, which is something we may be doing in this debate today.
The new President of the United States is facing a situation where he must demonstrate that the United States is in control of the situation and is in a position to counter certain influences from Cuba and from other parts of the world. In the long run this exercise will not be effective if it ignores the necessity of dismantling the unjust division of wealth and the menace created by unjust governments which take power and manage to remain in power. For the Americans to retain our support, it will be necessary for them to demonstrate to us and to other parts of the world that the United States is prepared to approach the situation in Central America with this kind of sensitivity to the social forces at play.
There is a certain dynamic in the El Salvadorian situation which is dangerously reminiscent of what has happened in other nations which have fallen prey to extremist governments. Therefore, it is useful that we have this debate today in the House. It gives us an opportunity to look at the situation against a much broader background. The background I would attempt to describe is a framework within which we can place a number of nations that are coming of age. They now have access to international means of communication such as radio and television. They are becoming aware of how different life can be under different circumstances. They are also the object

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
of propaganda competitions by various systems of government throughout the world. They are fertile ground for all forms of political activism which may not be so much local as imported. They are quick in taking root and developing momentum.
In that category you can place a number of nations, particularly if you look south toward Central and Latin America. We may be witnessing another step along the road of changes in power distribution whereby certain nations upon which the West has been able to count for a long time can no longer be taken for granted. The move toward establishment of certain basic principles, such as redistribution of wealth in very poor countries, may be such that it cannot be stopped by intervention from abroad.
Having listened to descriptions by other members, how can we accept the inequality of social conditions in a country like El Salvador? How can we accept the steps taken by the government there to maintain its power? Conditions such as those are repugnant to Canadians, yet we look at the situation with a sense of helplessness.
Because of the distance from Canada and the differences in culture, language and the like, we know that in the long run the solution must come from within that country. If the super powers are directly or indirectly involved, they can, if they wish, tilt the balance in their favour, but in the end, it will not bring about solutions of a lasting nature.
I am not saying that the situation in El Salvador and similar situations throughout the world can be resolved by outside forces. However, it will help if democratic countries such as Canada assist those countries to evolve and to adopt political parties such as we have. It would help if we supported the moderates in those countries, even though they are supposedly difficult to find. We should try to replace the conflict between ideological systems and goals of a social and economic nature. Otherwise, even though our intentions may be good, we will only be dealing with the symptoms and not with the root of the problems that have evolved over decades and indeed centuries.
The motion before us asks us at the same time to condemn and to urge. I doubt whether one could be effective by first condemning and then urging. One's intervention is considerably eroded if one indulges in condemnation and at the same time tries to convince one's neighbour of the correctness of their assessment. I would support the approach of placing full emphasis on and 100 per cent effort behind the act of urging.
While I disagree with the mover of the motion in this regard, the Leader of the New Democratic Party has done a service to this House by putting this motion forward on the eve of the arrival of President Reagan. It allows us to air our views on this issue. We can put forward the thought, which I believe reflects the majority in this House, namely that we should try to convince the Americans that what is at stake here is not just a power play, that the proper approach is improved social development.
I cannot state strongly enough the argument I have been trying to define this afternoon, namely that what we are
witnessing in El Salvador is not just a beginning, as it was not in the case of Cuba. We are witnessing a development which may have repercussions and a similar pattern of evolution in neighbouring nations in that part of the world.
We will regret it years from now if we do not register the importance of understanding the plight of the people in these countries. In essence it permits violence and conflict within their midst because of social and economic conditions that are unacceptable to any civilization. We feel very deeply about this.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment briefly on the remarks this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). It struck me as rather strange that, during a debate on a very sensitive, pressing and serious subject, the minister would use the occasion to indicate to Canada and the world that we have no business intervening in the affairs of Latin America or, indeed, South America. It is strange he would take that posture considering the very positive position taken when this party was the government with respect to the situation in Namibia. The minister said that because of our lack of expertise in Latin America, we are the last ones who should intervene. On other occasions we have intervened with a force and compassion that at times was scarcely human. Did we know more about that other situation than the current situation in Latin America? Certainly the answer is clear: we did not know any more, yet we took a positive role, produced positive results and made a significant contribution.
It surprised me, indeed shocked me, that the minister would so underestimate the capacity of professional Canadian diplomats and non-governmental people, as well as concerned members of this chamber and of others, in their attempt to lend stability to another part of the world.
I want to move to a perhaps slightly different vein, a slightly different route from that which has been followed by my colleagues in this debate to this point in time. Let me address myself to the question whether or not Canada and Canadians have a legitimate interest in that part of the world.
Surely we have a legitimate interest wherever in the world the rights and liberties of people are being trampled and cast to one side. Surely there is no doubt that the absence of morality, and the broader question of human privation and human suffering, demand the intervention of not only Canadians but every human being in order to alleviate, ease and correct the situation. Surely Canada falls into that category.
We have another interest as well. There is conflicting data before us provided by the debate taking place about whether the United States should continue to intervene militarily through the provision of arms, lethal weapons systems and whatnot. That is not an aspect of the debate I particularly want to get into, except to say that I share the concerns of the distinguished former secretary of state for external affairs, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald),
March 9, 1981

who has said, as have others, that the motion before us is somewhat deficient in that it criticizes and condemns only one side. The Leader of the New Democratic Party was quick to correct that by saying he had without equivocation included both sides. After following the debate in recent weeks and days in this Parliament, I find myself closer to the interpretation placed upon that by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, although I accept his clarification of what he intended.
The question is resolved depending on where you sit. It is too easy and shallow to make a decision based upon information you want to accept and interpret in support of your own particular point of view. The need for critical information grows. As this conflict grows, not only in El Salvador but as it grew in Nicaragua and as it is growing throughout the world, so grows our requirement to know and understand more about what is going on there and what is going on in the Caribbean basin, among the Commonwealth countries, those small, beautiful island nation states in that part of the world. It is important that we know and understand more about what is going on there, just as it is throughout South America. As the need for accurate and informed information grows-and it grows with urgency each passing day-so do Canada's responsibility and moral obligations grow to establish or achieve a method of collecting, analysing and acting upon accurate information. In that proportion our responsibility grows. We must do this because the luxury of failing to do so is no longer in our interest.
Perhaps to go beyond that, not only is this luxury as portrayed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs staying out of that part of the world one that we can afford no longer in our own self-interest in terms of trade, but it is a luxury we can no longer afford in terms of human privation and morality.
For the minister to argue, as he has in recent days and again here earlier this afternoon, that El Salvador is not a country of historic interest to Canadians is to admit a colossal and profound ignorance of historic events and a total misunderstanding of the interrelationships between Latin America, the island nations of the Caribbean and North America.
What happens in Latin America happens swiftly, as it does in the Caribbean and in South America. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. What happens there affects the entire intra-American basin.
Without debating the allegations flowing from both sides and the centre of that torn nation, or drawing a parallel with other revolutionary regimes throughout the Caribbean basin, Latin and South America and elsewhere, let me make three brief points.
First, there remains little doubt that we cannot of our own volition assess accurately what is going on and base actions of persuasion as a people, or as a mediator in the form of an informed and enlightened nation, unless and until the government takes the type of positive action suggested not only by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands but as well by the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle), the hon.
El Salvador
member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) and, perhaps along another path, by my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche). That suggestion must be followed.
Secondly, we must be careful in whatever approach we take to the problems in Latin and South America so as not to equate diplomatic measures with moral approval of all of the activities of either side, or with any of the sides or points of view, in these struggles for changing internal order. I think that is fundamental. We must not abandon people because we object to the activities in whole or in part of their governments. It is the people of the Caribbean, of South America and of Latin America with whom we have long, honourable and historic ties.
Finally, we must always remember that if we lose this identity and association with people, if we confuse it with diplomatic niceties or with our objections to the activities of certain regimes which can be described as horrendous, then in fact what we will have lost is security in a friendly part of the world.
We may not, without fear of question, any longer turn a deaf ear or blind eye to events in this part of the world. To those countries in the turmoil of change, to those countries with economies torn by the difficulties of change, to those countries with the internal capacity to earn dollars ravaged by security concerns and rising costs of energy, to those countries that find it difficult to fit into trade patterns and so on, we must always demonstrate in every way possible that their trust and confidence in a democratic way of life can be relied upon.
Today more than ever it is important to expand and nurture our relations with all neighbours to the south. I should like to elaborate further on the minister's denial of Canadian interests in that part of the world; I am sorry he is not present in the chamber at the moment. For example, does the minister believe for a minute that because El Salvador is on the Pacific coast, there is no direct linkage with its neighbours, good or bad, to the east? Is he suggesting that there is no relationship with Cuba? We have heard enough in recent weeks with respect to Cuba and the movement of arms through Costa Rica.
In that connection, and at the risk of embarrassing a very dear friend, I speak with first-hand knowledge of the movement of arms from Cuba, through Panama, into Costa Rica and on into El Salvador. Is the minister suggesting that there is no relationship with Cuba, given Cuba's relationship with Grenada? I find that hard to understand. Of course, Grenada is still closely linked, although it has suspended the option of consulting with the people as democracies are wont to do. Nevertheless, Grenada still enjoys Commonwealth ties. Do we not have an interest? Of course we have an interest.
Is the minister suggesting that we have no interest in Panama or the canal? Does he not know where El Salvador is in relationship to the approaches to the canal? Of course he does. Is the minister suggesting that we have no interest in Costa Rica or Guatemala, with their democratically-elected

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
governments? Is he suggesting that we have no interest in these nations? What about Honduras or Nicaragua? Surely the minister was not telling the House that we have no special interest in the OAS, of which El Salvador is still a member, though I do not know for how much longer. Is he suggesting that Canada is not the most active observer with respect to the OAS? Of course we are.
Surprise must be registered in the area of trade. Surely it is not necessary to tell the minister and the government that Latin and South American countries are increasing their trade with Canada, and Canada with them, at a far greater rate than with the United States. They are buying more and doing more business with us on a percentage basis than the United States.
For example, exports of metals, electrical equipment, telecommunications, prefabs, road building equipment, etc., from Canada to El Salvador increased from $13.5 million to some $15.6 million. One might say that is not very much, but let me put it in another context. Imports to Canada from El Salvador have virtually doubled. I should like to keep this in the context of Latin American countries in which the good professor has indicated that we have no historic interest. Of course we have an historical interest. Between 1968 and 1972 we have done $520.8 million worth of business with Latin American countries, a growth rate of 10.9 per cent. During the same period, our growth rate with respect to exports from Canada to the United States rose by only 9.5 per cent. The growth rate is there, the business interest is there. The growth rate has not come about by disinterested Canadian businessmen sitting in Canada and waiting for things to happen. We have a very serious interest in this matter. In fact, in the next two to two and a half years, foreign investment in these countries will rise from $1.6 billion to something in excess of $2 billion. We have large interests, we have small interests; we have humanitarian interests, we have economic interests.
We did not hesitate to donate $57,000 for medical clinics and ambulance services in El Salvador by way of aid through the International Red Cross when it was apparent that it was needed. We had no hesitation in giving somewhat similar aid to Nicaragua, some $67 million to protect prisoners of war and their families, not to mention that we respond whenever there is an earthquake, a hurricane or flooding; whenever there is need, we respond. We have a long, honourable history of response. It does not augur well for the minister to indicate that we must stay out of Latin America because we have no interest or historical ties in that area. We must remember the assistance of countless non-governmental organizations and their diversified programs, the financial contributions to multinational institutions and so on. These efforts speak not only loudly for the humanitarian concerns of Canadians, but they also reflect clearly our interest in this area of the world. This interest goes back well over 100 years in a very active sense and in excess of 270 years in particular instances.
At least the government should follow its own lead. The minister knows my strong support for whatever efforts he can make in the Caribbean, Latin America and South America. I
commend him for his efforts in recent months. Through his own initiative he has committed the government to closer ties with that part of the world, to expanding and increasing all forms of aid.
Let me conclude by indicating that no matter how far the Secretary of State for External Affairs may go, he will not have gone far enough until he has reached 25 per cent to 35 per cent of our total aid package.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very glad indeed to hear the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) say that the New Democratic Party had done a service by bringing this resolution before the House today. I found that his whole speech and approach on behalf of the government was a good deal more illuminating and thoughtful than was that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). However, I would like to say to the hon. member for Davenport that he did to a certain extent misread the motion which we are introducing today when he suggested that the motion was both condemning the United States for something and urging it to do something. If you look at the motion carefully, Mr. Speaker, you will see that what we are condemning is the hon. member's government. The motion reads quite clearly:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to protest publicly the American military intervention in support of the junta in El Salvador-
The motion then goes on to urge the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his talks with the President:
-to urge an end to this military involvement on the side of a regressive regime which denies civil rights and is fighting those who wish to establish a democratic government.
For the Secretary of State for External Affairs to say that the motion is "a calculated attempt to create tension between the Government of Canada and the government of the United States" would be laughable were it not so sad. The minister does not seem to realize that there are people, not only in Canada but all over the United States, in Latin America- Mexico and Venezuela particularly-and throughout other countries who are horrified by what is happening in El Salvador and by the escalation of American military aid to that junta. Perhaps this is what the minister meant when he said that he and his government had no expertise in this area.
Over the last weeks we have seen this concern raised in every city in Canada. It will be raised again in Ottawa tomorrow. Canadians cannot support this repressive regime any longer or the military aid which has been given to it. As I said a moment ago, it is not only Canadians who are concerned, but Americans in every city in that country as well. Some 52 congressmen are concerned. Indeed, within his own party President Reagan is now being challenged by the Republican minority leader of the House subcommittee on appropriations, Representative Conti, who has challenged the El Salvador military aid policy.
I wonder if the minister knows that three pieces of legislation will soon be brought before the American Congress in
March 9, 1981

attempts to change American military policy. The first of these is House of Representatives resolution number 1509, which is an amendment to the foreign assistance act of 1961. The amendment attempts to limit military aid, sales and credits.
Second, there is concurrent resolution No. 67 condemning all foreign involvement, including U.S. involvement, in El Salvador. It calls for a negotiated settlement and an end to U.S. military aid pending a review of that aid by the House committee on foreign affairs.
Third, there is the Ottinger resolution, which attempts to limit the President's powers to commit U.S. military personnel to foreign adventures. Senators Kennedy and Thongas said Friday that they will propose legislation this week in an effort to end U.S. military involvement in El Salvador.
The opposition to the U.S. government's policy in El Salvador is far stronger in the United States, in journals and magazines, as well as in the Congress of the United States, than it is on the part of the Government of Canada. The minister says that the motion is a calculated attempt to raise tension between Canada and the United States. Are all these criticisms of American policy which emanate from the U.S. Congress and the press not also of concern to him? With the minister's expertise in mind, does he not have any idea of the constituent elements in the democratic revolutionary front? Does he not know that it is an extraordinarily broad-based group with about 40 groups within it? Of course there are some communists in it; but there are also social democrats, socialists, conservatives, small businessmen, many Catholic priests, as he knows, and a large section of the church in El Salvador, the peasants organizations and labour unions. You cannot find any organization, in the labour movement, except one CIA-backed one, which is not supporting the democratic revolutionary front.
When Secretary Haig came to Canada and told our minister about the way he saw the situation in El Salvador, the minister accepted totally what he was told, without asking for any proof or evidence of the enormous volume of arms being sent in by Cuba, Nicaragua or the Soviet bloc. Indeed, the State Department has not yet published the evidence. It keeps telling us that it has evidence, but it seems very reluctant to publish it. Apparently, even the leader of the junta in El Salvador has not seen the evidence, since he has said nothing about it, not even to say that it exists. We need to know what it is.
A great many of us, including the minister I am sure, were led to believe a lot of "evidence" during the course of the Vietnam war, evidence also collected by the Central Intelligence Agency-evidence that turned out to be shoddy and untrue. Why do we not all say, "Let us have an investigation. Let us see what this outside intervention amounts to. Let there be a fair and impartial look. Let us not automatically accept something when we have not even seen the grounds on which it is based."
None of the documents has been made available. The leaders of Mexico, Venezuela and, indeed, every western European country that the State Department sent representatives to
El Salvador
visit, were very skeptical. Surely, as one of the best friends the United States has, it is our duty to raise our voices when we feel and think that the United States is pursuing a policy which could lead to another Vietnam. Surely it is not something from which we should hide. It is not something that we hope someone else will do. The point made by the minister that it is not Canada's concern, that we somehow can have no positive influence-as we can in Mexico, Brazil and Venezuela-is absolute nonsense. El Salvador is part of our hemisphere. El Salvador is closer to Ottawa, I believe, than Vancouver and has always been part of our hemisphere. The United States ambassador to the UN, Jeanne Kirkpatrick, says that what is happening with the American involvement is different from Vietnam because it is in this hemisphere. On television the other night she said that the difference is that it is taking place in this hemisphere. That is all the more reason for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to speak urgently, frankly and strongly of the opposition which we share with many elements in American society and government, with west-European countries and with many in Latin America itself. It is also our duty to look once again at the savagery of the right wing forces in El Salvador which have been encouraged directly or indirectly by the junta which governs the country.
We cannot simply dismiss 12,000 violent deaths. Even the former U.S. ambassador to El Salvador, Mr. White, said that 80 per cent of the deaths were the responsibility of government troops or troops under government protection. As compassionate human beings, we cannot turn a blind eye to that, as the minister seems to be doing. More military aid from the United States will mean more violence. As others have said this afternoon, the solution must be a political solution, even though Secretary Haig, according to his remarks the other day, seems to have turned his back on that possibility.
The government has fallen into the trap of wanting badly to get along with the President of the United States, hoping that the fisheries treaty can be restored, hoping that money will be provided for the northern part of the pipeline, and hoping that the Americans will not mind too much about the government's national energy policy, and it has almost succumbed not just to the temptation but to how it sees reality, namely, that what the government of the United States says and does will automatically be approved by the Government of Canada. This is not only doing a disservice to Canadians, but it is also doing a grave disservice to our friends in the United States who are themselves critical of American government policy. But then they turn around and find we are supporting, with a pull of our forelock, what the American administration wants every time. All of us have friends in the United States, and we know they are distressed by our actions and attitudes these days.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) mentioned today in the House that the NORAD agreement will be signed while President Reagan is here. That is an agreement about which there has been absolutely no discussion in the House of Commons. The minister's answers this afternoon

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
clearly did not address many of the serious questions raised by the standing committee, particularly about the role Canada might play in aerospace-rather than just air space-a matter which NORAD does not even cover in the present agreement. In fact, the present agreement does not cover any of the urgent matters relating to American military strategy.
In the course of making known our strong feelings about the military intervention in El Salvador, I suggest to the government that we also make known our strong feelings about certain developments in American military strategy generally, particularly the doctrine the Reagan administration has announced respecting nuclear superiority. We should pause before we sign that agreement. It does not have to be signed until May. I suggest there be a much more careful examination of all military developments emanating from the U.S. administration. Many, if not all, of them are basically outside the NORAD agreement, and we have absolutely no say about them at all. This was even admitted by the commander-inchief of NORAD, General Hartinger at Colorado Springs when he agreed that effectively we did not or could not have any say. When asked why our presence is valued, he said it is to show the rest of the world that we share American military strategies. Well, we do not share the American strategy nor, as I have pointed out, do great numbers of Americans share American strategy in relation to El Salvador. That is why we brought this motion forward today and why every speaker so far, including speakers from the government side, with the exception of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, have urged that a military solution in El Salvador is no solution.

speechtext:

Above all, we do not share their escalating intervention in a country racked by the very terrorism which, when he first became secretary of state, General Haig said would become the top priority in American foreign policy.
