subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members opposite have repeated today the same criticisms about Canada's policy concerning El Salvador as were voiced in recent days during Oral Question Period and on March 2 during the adjournment debate. They are complaining that we do not have any policy or that our policy is inconsistent or contradictory. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) explained very clearly during the adjournment debate that this government has been following a clear and consistent policy since its election. In his comments today, he gave a more detailed explanation of this policy, and I hope that the opposition members will now understand to what extent their criticisms are unfounded. It has been clearly stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the government is opposed to any foreign intervention in El Salvador and that the population of that country should be allowed to solve its social and political conflicts on its own, by peaceful and democratic means.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that all the members of this House can support this policy and I see no need to dwell any further on this subject. In Canada as in other countries, there are people who are inclined to consider the conflict in El Salvador as a classical example of the political rivalry that exists between East and West. However, in his statement today, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated that such were not the views held by the Canadian government. In its opinion, the basic problem in El Salvador stems out of the need for social and economic justice within a population which has for too long been refused any hope for a better life.
Because it has an industrious, progressive and homogeneous population, El Salvador has managed to achieve a certain amount of progress in facing the challenges of the twentieth century, but this country is also a quite eloquent example of one of the most difficult problems of this century, that is, overpopulation. El Salvador is now the most densely populated country and the one with the lowest per capita income in Central America, and its economic and social development has been severely hindered by this situation. Where the political development of El Salvador is concerned, nothing much more impressive is to be noted. In his book entitled "A History of Latin America From the Beginnings to the Present", historian Hubert Herring reports the following:

In El Salvador presidents come and go, civil wars rage briefly, and moderate dictatorships are the general pattern . . . But the social pattern of El Salvador remains undisturbed. No nation in Latin America presented a greater contrast than between the few Salvadoran families who lived in luxury, sent their sons to schools abroad, and drove fine sports cars-and the masses who are ragged and illfed. The chief families-the 'fourteen families' they were popularly called, although there were more than fourteen-hold the most land and the best land: it was estimated in 1961 that less than 0.1 per cent of the landholders owned
March 9, 1981

some 16 per cent of the farmland, in haciendas of 2,471 acres or more; while at the other extreme about 85 per cent of the farmers, holding less than 15 per cent of the farmland, were hard put to make a living from the meagre plots of 12.4 acres or less, working without machinery or scientific handling of seeds and fertilizers. The great plantations were officially run, but the humble workers on those plantations were lucky to get the equivalent of 50-60 cents a day, plus meagre rations of tortillas and beans. And the military leaders were not ready to break their long alliance with the country's elite, which had been effective in throttling social legislation. They had agreed to keep the poor in their place; and although the poor were beginning to awake-some turning to communism which flourished in a few labour unions-government administration still found it unwise to push social security, public health measures, and agrarian reform.
[ Translation]
The early thirties were marked with violence as the economic impact of the world depression led the peasants to revolt and consequently to the brutal repression which made thousands of victims, if I may open a brief parenthesis, Mr. Speaker, I would add that Canada was marginally involved in the events which occurred in El Salvador at the time as two Canadian destroyers, HMCS Vancouver and HMCS Skeena, under Commander Victor G. Brodeur, were dispatched to the coastal town of Acajutla "to protect, if required, foreign interests", as reported in the media at that time. It is also interesting to note that, in his subsequent report to Ottawa, Commander Brodeur stated the following:

The revolution was entirely due to lack of consideration for the Indians. There are only two classes in El Salvador, i.e. the very rich and the Indians. The very rich are very few and it is noticeable that these few left the country the minute the trouble started.
[ Translation]
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the situation in El Salvador had not changed much over the years. Therefore it is not surprising that political and social agitation has become endemic in that small country and that the workers in farms and cities rose against the long domination by prominent families and the military. On October 26, 1960, the world witnessed the first serious attempt to correct past wrongs, something which indeed turned out to be a harbinger of what is happening now. The government at the time was overturned by a group of leftist officers and civilians, but the six-man junta in power proved to be overly radical for most of the El Salvador officers and was in turn overthrown in another coup in January, 1961. Again may I quote professor Herring:

The new junta, headed by Colonel Julio Adelberto Rivera . . . promised early elections and a speedy return to constitutional government. . . During the first 270 days of the junta's reign, 325 decree laws were promulgated, and they attacked many of the obvious inequities in El Salvador's ill-balanced society. These measures . . . included an income tax decree establishing the top levy of 76.5 per cent on incomes above $70,000. This law also tackled the knotty problem of the flight of capital, by providing tax exemption for money used for private investment in El Salvador, while taxing uninvested capital at a higher rate. The income tax law was a sensational move, evoking throaty charges of 'communism' against the highly respected military junta . . . There was a furious exchange of manifestos between defenders and opponents of the measure. The ruling junta defended its course by saying that its policy was inspired by the obvious ills of the citizenry-'malnutrition, illiteracy, high index of infant mortality, bare feet, semi-naked bodies, filthy tenements, long and exhausting working hours, and wages of hunger.'
El Salvador

The promised elections were held in April 1962. Colonel Rivera was elected for a five-year term until 1967. Professor Herring continues as follows:
Forthwith the reforms launched by the junta began to take shape. High priority was given to agrarian reform; although densely populated, El Salvador has little available land for colonization; some state-owned land plus some privately held farms would furnish about 135,000 acres to be distributed to some 3,500 families in plots ranging from 5.25 acres to 14 acres; it was not a very bold program but at least it was a beginning. There were various measures for easing the burden on the poor: Sunday rest with pay; minimum wage laws; reduction of rent on tenements; provision for more generous food allowances for workers on the large farms. The new income taxes were enforced with considerable success. Banking laws were reformed making credit more easily available to small farmers. And government operations were honest.

In the 1967 presidential elections Fidel Sanchez Hernandez was victorious with 54.4 per cent of the votes and his administration continued Colonel Rivera's reform program. His policies included an agricultural reform project which greatly upset the conservative businessmen and the rich land owners. Then a great controversy surrounded the 1972 elections when a member of the Christian Democrat Party, El Salvador's current president Jose Napoleon Duarte, apparently rallied the majority of the votes. However, a subsequent official recount gave the majority to Colonel Arturo Molina. He was president until 1977 when the military resorted to similar tactics during the presidential elections and brought General Carlos Romero to power. Riots broke out as a result of that disloyal manoeuvre and the government imposed martial law; before order was restored about one hundred protesters had been killed.
President Romero was an inveterate conservative who associated social reform with communism; supported by the military, the conservative aristocracy resisted the peasants' claims for social and agrarian reform. Violence became commonplace; groups of vigilantes and rightist paramilitary tortured and executed the leaders of peasant groups and other partisans of economic and social reform. Naturally, that violence provoked leftist reactions. The intensity of the struggle between the two factions increased, and President Romero led a fierce campaign against the left and its followers.
On October 15, 1979, 19 years almost to the day after the reformist junta which I have already mentioned seized power, a group of Liberal army officers deposed Romero after a coup d'Etat whose victims were few and put in its stead a progressive junta composed of two Liberal officers, two members of the Christian Democrat Party and one Independent. As mentioned by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his statement, the new government promised to implement radical reforms in the field of social and economic affairs, the most important of which was an agrarian reform in two steps comparable to that implemented in Mexico. The first stage, started in March of 1980, involved all agricultural operations

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
of over ! ,234 acres; some 400 properties representing 600,000 acres, that is, about 25 per cent of all farmlands in the country, were redistributed amongst the peasants.
The second phase, which is to be implemented in 1981, is aimed at all farms of 370 to 1,235 acres. Unfortunately, left-wing groups immediately took advantage of the situation to try and foster a revolution. They launched a terrorist campaign which included the kidnapping and murder of several Salvadorian and foreign businessmen and bankers and, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned in his remarks, attacks on embassies and the kidnapping and murder of embassy staff. This resulted in the closing of a large number of Salvadorian and foreign plants, a 50 to 60 per cent decrease in industrial production as well as a corresponding chop in employment and a worsening of the situation for Salvadorian workers. In the last two years, 28 embassies were attacked by terrorists so that all west European countries, except Italy, were forced to close their embassies there.
It seems clear that as long as the extreme left in El Salvador had taken Romero, the military dictator, as its target, its chances of success were quite good. However, the reformist junta, with its land, business and banking reforms and its promise to hold an election within two years, sabotaged the strategy of the extreme left and destroyed its hopes of coming to power. It is interesting to note that the extreme left rejected the junta's platform without even giving it a chance to implement it. However, leftist attacks were not the only problems faced by the junta. It also faced the opposition of conservative elements within the military and the security forces as well as the opposition of those whose direct interests were threatened by reformist action and who tried to undermine the junta's ability to govern. Then, there was the terrible war of attrition between the armed sectors of left-wing and right-wing factions. The government was caught in the crossfire and became increasingly unable to control its destiny.
Mr. Speaker, I have given the background to the events which have occurred in El Salvador because I think it is important that we keep them in mind when considering the present situation. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs so correctly noted today, we must consider the crisis in the context of the past problems experienced by El Salvador. The tragedy lies in the fact that conflicts between the extreme right and the extreme left have taken unimaginable proportions; violent acts and murders are committed by armed gangsters, soldiers, revolutionaries and criminals on both sides, the government and its supporters being the targets more often than not. We are constantly informed by the media of these terrible crimes and atrocities which fill us all with the greatest repulsion. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated that the Canadian government has brought pressure to bear on several occasions on the Salvadorian government to keep its army, police and security forces as well as paramilitary extremists under greater control, to put an end to these human rights violations and bring the guilty before the courts.
Apparently, President Duarte is trying to exert such control. Unfortunately, his efforts are too few and too late. Maybe the Salvadorian government could not, however, do any more than it did. We must keep on urging it to act more efficiently, and I was happy to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs state his intention to keep the pressure on.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to follow my colleagues in the House in addressing the tragic situation in El Salvador and in seeking to encourage the government toward a positive approach which we as a nation might play in seeking an end to the bloodbath which currently is a day by day experience there. We hdard from the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) some proposals which we might adopt in terms of being a peacemaker or mediator in that situation. My colleague for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) reminded us of the quality of human suffering that is part of that tragedy and of our common humanity. The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) reminded us of our national interest and the interdependence which we have with the people of the Americas and the people of El Salvador.
This evening I would like, in the few moments that are mine in this debate, to turn my thoughts to the fact that we in Canada have a special interest. I want to take issue with the minister and his comments to us last Monday evening in the House that we do not have the right to comment, that we are not in a position to pass judgment on the political situation there and, therefore, we ought not as a nation take part in a moral discussion about the future of the human family and of our hemisphere.
I am reminded of our Canadian tradition of welcoming refugees, and the political judgment which goes with it, from the actions of governments which have, in many cases, expelled or forced out their nationals. I am reminded of the position of the government on disarmament, and the appointment of an ambassador for disarmament; of the matter of giving priority to disarming, and the moral positions that have been taken.
I wish to remind the House of our Canadian history in relation to the founding and developing of the United Nations and, through it, the setting up of peacekeeping mechanisms. Therefore, it is with a great deal of distress that I find the
March 9, 1981

government is suggesting through the minister that we do not have the right to comment. He is suggesting in this case of real concern to Canadians that, "given our lack of close involvement with El Salvador for generations, we are in no position to pass judgment on the political situation in that country."
I wish to suggest to this House and the government that all across Canada we have a very real constituency of concern. It expects this government to echo our concern for human rights and reflect the deep distress of Canadians at the ongoing, day by day account of the 25 or more people found assassinated each night in the streets.
Let me share with the House a letter which was addressed on March 5 to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with a copy to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan) from the Canadian Council of Churches. The letter reads in part:
We, the representatives of the members of the Canadian Council of Churches, wish to convey our serious concern about human rights. We decided to write to you on the eve of the impending visit of President Reagan, whose statements on foreign policy clearly indicate a change in policy and practice on human rights by the United States administration-
As you are aware, the churches in Canada often have intimate and personal knowledge of the situation at the grass-roots level in many countries through their partnership with the churches in those parts of the world. We wish to continue to share this knowledge with our government in order that Canada can play a significant role in creating a more humane world. Precisely because we are nqt a super power, we are in an excellent position to align ourselves with other nations to work together for the protection of the rights of people who are used, oppressed and sometimes murdered . . . We note with pleasure Mr. Mac-Guigan's remarks made before church representatives on January 28, 1981 to the effect that human rights are the highest concern for the Canadian government; that it is a personal priority for him as minister; and that Canada will continue to act in defence of human rights on moral grounds, alone if necessary .. . We expect our government to stand firm on the position it took at the time Canada voted in the United Nations for the Resolution 53/192 in December, 1980 calling on governments to refrain from the supply of arms and other military assistance to El Salvador. We know for a fact that the present regime in the country is responsible for deaths of thousands of people-
We sincerely hope, sir, that Canada will continue to play a leading role in the struggle for the world where fundamental human rights take precedence over national security and balances of power.
This is signed not only by officers of the Canadian Council of Churches, but also by senior officers of the Anglican Church, the Baptist Convention, the Christian Church (Disciples), the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Lutheran Church, the Reformed Church in America, the Religious Society of Friends, the United Church of Canada and the Presbyterian Church in Canada.
I want to suggest there is a constituency there which is aware of, and in contact with, the people of El Salvador and is sharing in the situation and looking for the moral support which Canada has traditionally given, ought to be giving at this time and ought to be communicating to her close friends, especially our very close and good friends in the United States.
In October, the United Church of Canada through its publication, the Observer, had an entire issue on "The Heroic Church in Central America". They began that presentation with a letter from the Salvadorian Episcopal Conference dated
El Salvador
March 5, 1977. These were the words of the conference at that time:
Even at the risk of being persecuted or misunderstood, the Church cannot avoid raising her voice when injustice has taken hold of society. She cannot remain silent when human rights are trampled upon, whether in institutionalized form or in concrete cases-
The author of that article, Mr. Hugh McCullum, went on in an opening comment to say:
What you do not understand in North America is that people here are prepared to die for the simple freedoms you take for granted-like freedom to live.
The story goes on to refer to the body of information which has been brought into question by the minister as to whether there are facts upon which Canadians build their concern. At one point, editor McCullum lists:	-
Fact-finding missions of British Members of Parliament, the Organization of American States (OAS), Amnesty International, an American ecumenical delegation, and ICCHRLA-organized visit by Canadian churches, as well as the Salvadorian Human Rights Commission-
It goes on to chronicle the number of groups which have concurred in their evidence of what is the situation there.
Lest we in Canada, at some distance away from Central America as some may feel, think that we are not in communication, let the House be reminded of the communication, dated January 1, 1981, which came ecumenically from Christian groups across El Salvador as an open letter to the Christian community and, indeed, to Canadians as a whole, speaking about their part in this struggle. Since there has been so much discussion about the radical left and the radical right, let us remember that the important element in the community is the vast majority of people who find themselves very often represented by Christian groups concerned with the wholeness of life, whether it be health care, agriculture or medical care. That group writes in its letter:
For years we have been close to the suffering people, to the poor and oppressed; we have experienced their misery but also their hope and their decision for an authentic liberation.
The church there says: "we want to be with the poor", and it makes three points. The first point is:
For 50 years the Salvadorean people has lived under oppression of gravely unjust economic, social and political structures, which in no wise have promoted the common good of the poor majorities-
It goes on to state:
Human rights have been systematically violated under military regimes of national security.
The letter goes on to state:
The Church has also been persecuted-
Later it states:
This government, consequently, is not legitimate. It does not seek nor secure the common good-
Secondly, the letter says to us in Canada:
The Salvadorean people has not chosen armed conflict; but rather conflict has been imposed on it. Over the years it has sought peaceful solutions in elections and used social and political pressure to achieve its aspirations. Everything has proved futile.

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
The letter goes on to state:
-the United States is not supported by any right to interfere in the destiny of El Salvador in order to determine its future and still less to support militarily the current government.
This is the third point in the letter, Mr. Speaker:
An insurrection for the liberation of a people is not only a legitimate historical reality, but, for Christians, it is also a sign of the times through which God speaks to and calls us. The first thing that a just uprising tells us is that God's patience has run out. The experience of Israel and Egypt is being repeated-
This pastoral letter, which came at the turn of the year to Canada, ends with these words:
With faith in God and in the blood shed by so many Salvadorian martyrs, we would like to end with the prophetic words of Monsenor Romero that we may not falter: "The cry of liberation of this people is a cry that reaches up to God and one that nothing and no one can stop." Over these ruins the glory of the Lord will shine.
I could go on and quote from a letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) of February 19 from the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops which again confirms the evidence sent to us by the Christian community there, and coincides with other evidence we have before us.
I could go on and read into the record evidence from the Inter-Church Committee on Human Rights in Latin America which, on December 3, 1980, presented a brief, documenting sources, to the Secretary of State for External Affairs on Canadian relations with the Republic of El Salvador. In that brief, they gave substantive evidence of the broad spectrum of persecution and denial of human rights, and they went on to speak about the effect on Canadians of the assassination of Bishop Romero. They refer to the fact-finding visits and frequent communications which have been a part of our experience and the shared concern of Canadians from Victoria to St. John's.
Already during this debate we have been reminded of our Canadian position which was authorized by this government, that is, to vote in favour of the words that Canada "calls upon governments to refrain from the supply of arms and other military assistance in the current circumstances;".
It is interesting to note that Canada was among 70 which voted for that; there were only 12 who voted against it, including the present government of El Salvador, and 55 which abstained, including the United States.
Ambassador White has already been quoted several times during this debate, but in case one thinks it is only the church community which is concerned, we also have the record of diplomatic reports, and we have already rehearsed in this House the concern of other Central and Latin American nations and the concern of West Germany and France. We have signed declarations with Venezuela and Mexico as a nation about concern for this supply of arms to that area.
We are reminded again in The New York Times of Ambassador White's comments as follows:
To the extent that you emphasize a military solution in El Salvador, you are going to be buttressing one of the most out-of-control, violent, bloodthirsty groups of men in the world. They have killed-at a minimum-5,000 or 6,000 kids, just on the mere suspicion that they were involved with the leftists.
One could also read into the record the testimony of Oxfam, a voluntary agency from the United States, and its comment on the agrarian reform. The minister, in his intervention, laid great emphasis on the slow but steady effectiveness of agrarian reform. Oxfam, U.S.A., reports:
Over 60 per cent of El Salvador's rural population are not potential beneficiai-ries for the current land reform program.
The current land reform program excludes the poorest and largest section of the rural population-landless rural labourers.
The peasantry. Church, academics, and agrarian experts of El Salvador have been excluded from the design, planning and implementation of the current agrarian reform.
The land reform program has been implemented in the context of increasing and unrelenting levels of violence against the rural population.
They go on to suggest that this program should not be given the credibility which, in debate, some seek to give it.
One week ago tonight, Mr. Speaker, in raising questions on El Salvador following question period, I proposed that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence be called and that expert witnesses from the news media, international and Canadian, voluntary agencies, from the business and church communities be called in order that the division of opinion which has been raised by the minister, and the suspicion that there are divisions between the Vatican and the bishops, be tested in order that we can continue a positive and affirmative approach as Canadians for human rights.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to be with those who think it is important that Canada light a candle rather than curse the darkness of our world. We have an enviable record as a peacekeeper and peacemaker. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has suggested that Canada take the initiative by contacting neighbouring states, and that we take the initiative to see that an international body, either through the United Nations or through other groups, be invited and encouraged to seek a political solution.
I believe it is important for Canadians to respond, in the wake of the visit of the President of the United States, with their concerns. I believe that telegrams, telephone calls and letters ought to be sent to the Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs saying that Canada ought to continue its stand on disarmament and political solutions, and continue to stand for human rights in our world.
I want to suggest that if we are not prepared to initiate some international mechanisms which can bring forth that information, then let us ourselves, as Canadians, invite from all parties in this House those who will go along with representatives of the voluntary agencies, churches and the news media, and let us send a task force which will return and report to this House and to the Canadian people as to whether it is just a simple issue of left versus right, or whether this is a legitimate rising of expectations by people who want their freedom and their rights. Let the task force examine the great body of evidence from the voluntary agencies, the international news media and the churches, or whether we are being tempted to think that.
March 9, 1981

because there are communist elements and right-wing elements, somehow these are dominant and the great interests of others are lost.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me suggest to you that we as Canadians have a proud tradition of seeking peaceful solutions and we would wish to be seen, in our conversations with our closest ally and friend, pressing them to pursue that direction in the world of human affairs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) has put before the House an important matter, and 1 think the thoughtful tone of the speeches today has indicated how seriously it is taken on all sides of the House. We see in our time the most appalling violations of human rights and incredible savagery by governments against their own nationals. Unfortunately we see this in dictatorships of the left and the right; no ideology has a particular claim to morality.
In the case of El Salvador, on March 2 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) listed a number of steps that have been taken by Canada in pursuit of our general commitment to work constructively with other nations for human rights. On many occasions, through the Organization of American States, the United Nations and its agencies, and in bilateral talks with the government of El Salvador in midi Kebruary, the Government of Canada made representations on behalf of human rights in that country.
We have consistently proclaimed our support for peace in the world and our opposition to the supply of offensive arms to El Salvador by outside sources, whether from communist or non-communist countries.
We have consistently insisted on the importance and necessity of a political, not military, solution in El Salvador. We have made it clear that we do not see ourselves or any other country imposing that political solution on that country, or favouring one side or the other, that this is a matter for the nationals of that country to resolve themselves.
This same position has been taken by countries very close to El Salvador, such as Mexico and Venezuela. On pages 7817 and 7818 of Hansard, there are listed accounts of a number of initiatives, which I will not repeat now, of joint Canada-Mex-ico, Canada-Venezuela and Canada-Brazil communications, all expressing the hope that El Salvador could achieve peace, democracy and social justice, and also expressing opposition to any kind of foreign intervention. So, Canada's position is clear and consistent.
The NDP motion before us offers no proposals or recommendations to bring about an end to the violence in El Salvador, except to protest a decision of the United States government to supply military equipment. The motion is onesided because concern has not been expressed about the receipt of arms by left-wing guerrillas and their use in contributing to the violence and tragic loss of life.
The motion also calls on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his talks with the President of the United States, to urge an end to American military intervention. The Prime Minister
El Salvador
and Secretary of State for External Affairs have already explained many times publicly that our government's policy is one of opposition to military intervention by any country, whether it be the United States or a communist-bloc or any other country. This has been the government's policy for many months, stated many times and was repeated today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
If the New Democratic Party wishes to have a resolution passed which might play a constructive role in bringing about a settlement of the tragedy of El Salvador, why does the motion not call on the Prime Minister or Secretary of State for External Affairs, in addition to discussing the matter with the President of the United States, to appeal to the leaders of the revolutionary groups in El Salvador? The Secretary of State for External Affairs has explained that he made Canada's position clear to representatives of the revolutionary force whom he met in Ottawa a few weeks ago. I understand that some hon. members opposite also met with those representatives at that time, and I hope that they conveyed to them the need to follow the road of peace and negotiation.
In the House on March 2 the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) said:
-the only resort of the people of that country to deal with a vicious military regime is to take counter military action.
This remark puzzles me greatly. I find it difficult to understand a politician apparently recommending that people should continue to exercise violence, whatever the provocation. Surely as politicians we should try to negotiate and to find solutions by words, not by military action.
Canada does not have an embassy in El Salvador. Sometimes it is difficult for us to be clear about the exact situation inside that country, but we can look at the chronology of some of the events which have taken place in El Salvador since the Romero government was overthrown on October 15, 1979. These events have been reported rather extensively. At that time the new government promised social reforms. On October 25, 1979, the composition of the cabinet was announced. Two days later, left wing violence, rioting and looting began, with two government ministries occupied by leftist forces. The question that comes to mind is: Why, after only two days, did leftist guerrillas decide that these promised reforms would not be forthcoming and that it was necessary to begin to respond by violence?
Throughout November, bombings and violence continued. On November 28 left wing revolutionary groups kidnapped the South African ambassador. Throughout December and into January, 1980, violence increased to the point that the British embassy felt it had no alternative but to close. In February 1980, revolutionary groups occupied the Spanish embassy. During that month, the German government announced its intention of closing its embassy. The violence continued throughout February and March and a state of siege was declared on March 6. On March 24, Archbishop Romero was murdered while saying mass, and even his funeral on March

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
30 was disrupted by fire bombs and shootings. The leftists blamed the military and the rightists, while the government blamed the leftists, and the state of siege was extended for another 30 days.
Nevertheless, some reforms were pursued; at the end of April, sharecroppers and tenant farmers were given title to the land they worked.
The violence continued throughout the summer and autumn of 1980. On October 9, the South African ambassador, still a hostage of the left wing forces, died. Ten other assassination attempts were made; some successful, some not. On November 27, six leading members of the opposition were murdered. On December 4, the bodies of four American churchwomen were found in a shallow grave near the airport. On December 13, the junta was reorganized and Napoleon Duarte was named president. On January 10, the "final offensive" of the left wing began with widespread fighting and the calling of national strikes.
Nobody in the House denies that much of the violence, the murdering and the torturing, as far as we can see, was caused by right wing forces. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and other members have spoken plainly about this; but the resolution would seem to imply that the killings were caused only by the El Salvador government. While it is not easy to be clear about what exactly is happening, it is certainly clear that violence begets violence. Clearly no one is blameless in this terrible situation. The House should not be asked to approve a resolution which fails to take into account that there are, as always, two sides to a story, both of which in this case make very unpleasant reading.
The resolution before us also indicates that the left wing forces are the only ones wishing to establish a democratic government. The record would lead one to question this. The government of El Salvador has taken some steps to institute reform. In so doing, it has antagonized forces on the right and forces on the left. We all agree that the progress made has not been as swift or as significant as we would like to see, and I am sure that the people of El Salvador would like to see. But, despite the necessity of dealing with a continuing series of armed attacks, occupations, murders, assassinations and strikes, the government of El Salvador has been able to implement, albeit haltingly, some of its promised reforms.
There is no evidence to suggest that given a period of peace and tranquility, the government of El Salvador might not proceed to implement its reforms. If left wing sources are as determined to establish a democratic government, as the resolution would have us believe, why have they been so active in seeking to achieve power by brutal force against a regime which has publicly declared its intention to establish reforms?
No one on this side of the House has any illusions that the present government of El Salvador is perfect; far from it. Its imperfections are clear for all to see, but its imperfections are admitted by its leaders. They admit that greater efforts must be made to eliminate those imperfections. We have not heard that the leadership of the revolutionary forces admits any imperfections, but, as far as we can see, they urge their
followers to greater violence. The revolutionary forces have shown no great desire to work for a ceasefire and no willingness to negotiate toward a democratic settlement.
The president of El Salvador publicly expressed his willingness to negotiate with responsible leaders of the revolutionary forces. I hope those leaders with take up that challenge and seek to settle the differences in El Salvador with ballots rather than bullets. When the Secretary of State for External Affairs met the revolutionary leaders and sought their views, I understand they said that they were interested only in a discussion with the United States and that the discussions were only to persuade the United States to stop all military and economic assistance to El Salvador, so that revolutionary forces could overthrow the government.
It is hard to reconcile that view with the statement contained in the resolution of the New Democratic Party that the revolutionary leaders wish to establish a democratic government.
The Canadian government's policy has been clear and consistent throughout. We all care very deeply that there should be peace in that unfortunate country and that this senseless killing should stop. I certainly support the government's policy of objecting to the supply of military equipment by any and all countries to any and all parties in El Salvador. I support the government's position in using every opportunity to urge the government of El Salvador to put an end to abuses of human rights and to work toward a peaceful, negotiated settlement of the difficulties.
I support the Canadian government's activity in making its view known to other countries by discussions through diplomatic channels, but it is hard to see that the course suggested in this resolution would do anything to help matters.
This resolution contains two rather contradictory elements, one in which the Government of Canada is condemned for failing to protest publicly the American policy while, at the same time, we are asked to urge an end to military involvement on the part of the United States. It is difficult to see how, in the course of a state visit from an ally, our neighbour and friend, we can both urge and persuade, if that is what the NDP would have us do, while also prejudging and pre-empting the discussions by making public statements beforehand.
The resolution before the House is a flawed resolution, but it has served a useful purpose today by making us all think more deeply about the tragic state of affairs in El Salvador. It has made us think about the tragic denial of human rights in many other countries and the need for us to be vigilant and to use the international forums to express our convictions on every possible occasion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that tonight I am part of an historical moment in our country's history. I am proud to be able to speak for my party on this resolution. I have been in the House of Commons for almost two years now and up until tonight there has not been a debate
March 9, 1981

on external affairs. This is true of the party which sits opposite and true of the party to my right. The people of Canada have not had an opportunity, through their members, until tonight, to speak about any subject whatsoever as it relates to the external direction of our country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: You could have taken your day.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
I am happy tonight to have an opportunity to speak not only for Canadians, who I believe have not had their right fulfilled to hear about where our country is going externally, but at the same time to speak for millions of people who are not able to speak of conditions which they themselves no longer control-the oppressed people, millions of them all over the world who would like to have the opportunity to stand up in a free assembly like this and speak to the subjects which are keeping them, their families and, for all they know, their future families, in a state of slavery.
As a member of this House, 1 am happy to have the opportunity tonight to be able to speak freely. At the same time 1 believe I also speak for many friends of mine who are Americans, who no longer have this same ability to get up and, in a very clear way, criticize what is happening to part of our continent, as the member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) put it. In a particular way I would like to speak for the poor, the oppressed, the people who are living in slums, the people who are living in hide-outs in jungles, and the people who can no longer speak for themselves because of the frustrating oppression which has kept them in those places.
I would like to begin my remarks by reading into the record a message which was prepared by a wide sector of church groups in El Salvador. I feel that it is interesting for us tonight to give pause for a moment to say what the words "El Salvador" mean. "El Salvador" means The Saviour. The people there have a Christian tradition of almost 400 years. The capital of their country was called Holy Saviour and their country is called The Saviour. In this letter they are asking for salvation in a very special way. The letter reads as follows:
The people of El Salvador is living a critical and decisive hour of its history. It is deciding its future and destiny as a people. It is deciding to liberate itself from oppression, to regain its dignity, and to organize a society that will be fraternal and just for the poor majorities. In these moments the Salvadorian people is preparing itself for an insurrection as a last resort to obtain that justice and peace for which it has so yearned and which have so many times been denied it.
We as Christian, men and women religious, clergy, who work in the diverse areas of pastoral ministry, education, social development, and humanitarian aid, want also to accompany the people in these moments, acknowledge the justice of its cause and its struggle, and recognize the legitimate right which moves it to insurrection.
For years we have been close to the suffering people, to the poor and oppressed; we have experienced their misery but also their hope and their decision for an authentic liberation. We have attempted to serve them according to the Gospel, but they also have showed us the ultimate truth of the Gospel- the love of God as the good news of the kingdom for the poor. In this hour of insurrection, full of suffering and hope, we want to be with the poor, we want to explain our option, and we want to see in the insurrection of the people the very signs of the times, the word that God addresses us as Christians.
I will not read the whole letter. It was prepared on January 1 of this year by the Archdiocesan CARITAS of El Salvador, the Conference of Men and Women Religious of El Salvador,
El Salvador
the Federation of Centers of Catholic Education, the Archdiocesan Pastoral Council, the Baptist Assembly and the Christian Student Movement and others on an ecumenical base in El Salvador.
Tomorrow our country is welcoming the President of the United States. President Reagan is beginning a term of office. He, like many others, is beginning without a great deal of experience with respect to the responsibilities he must carry out in that role. I believe I state what many others believe-he does not have a great deal of experience in dealing with international matters. He has come out, or seems to have come out, of a life in which things were, to put it very simply, black or white.
If I can refer to his past history, it is not unlike a few poor cowboy movies on which one side there are white hats and on the other side there are black hats. You know from the beginning that the side with the white hats is all right and the side with the black is all wrong. It can be likened to cowboys and Indians, or G.I.s and Japs. It was so easy then, when the situation was clearly right or clearly wrong.
But places like El Salvador, Central America, Latin America and other countries in the developing world are not blacks or whites. They encompass a complex reality of all kinds of things-economic, social, religious and cultural. There, things do not come out black and white; they come out very grey. It requires a great deal of prudence and sensitivity to be able to make good judgments there. However, if one is moved by love and if one has a sense of justice, then those decisions will come with time, with listening and feeling. But it just cannot be said that they are right wing, left wing, communist or capitalist. Those names do not work. They are talking about the majority of people who no longer have the power to do anything except let the power of history flow over them or who finally say "No, I would rather die than let that happen."
I think the debate on El Salvador we are having tonight pinpoints another important reality of what our country and other countries are becoming more deeply involved with. It is the North-South reality. They are two little code words which do not seem to mean much to many people, simply because they are still new code words. The North refers basically to those countries which are more or less economically developed. The South refers basically to those countries which are in the process of development. In general, the North is above the equator, and the South below.
El Salvador is part of the South. It is one of the countries struggling to develop. It is not unlike other Latin American countries in which there has been institutionalized oppression of the poor. Its mode of developing will be different than that in other countries, but it must be respected. It cannot be opposed from an outside power, whether from the left, right, or anywhere else. The people there will have to make the decisions which will finally free them from the oppression of poverty which has put them in this situation.
8052

March 9, 198
El Salvador
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has indicated by his words and actions that he is very interested in this question of North-South. I trust that he is telling us the truth because it is the most important question now facing our planet. However, I would like to advise the Prime Minister that in the question of North-South, it is not only important to be able to talk about the situation but it is also important that we appear credible in the situation. We must be authentic, credible and serious.
The Prime Minister has made several tours to various developing countries preparing for the North-South encounters of this coming summer. I do not believe those trips were well prepared. I believe the trip to Brazil, for instance, was not well prepared. If we are not credible, there could be a problem.
One of the witnesses who appeared before the North-South committee task force was Maria Helena Moreira Alves, a Brazilian social worker who is now studying in the United States. She explained to us in committee that during his trip to Brazil the Prime Minister did not see the right people. It is true that he saw government officials, but he did not see leaders of the church who are much closer to the reality. He did not see people in the labour movement or those in the very vital Brazilian press who write about how they see real development.
The Brazilian problem, although much larger than the El Salvadorian problem, has many of the same aspects. From my own personal experience, I now know that the situation of 30 million to 40 million Brazilians is worse than it was 15 years ago. The "economic miracle", as they call Brazil, did not finally help the poor. The poor are now no longer eating the minimum of rice and beans; they are now down to eating rice and are no longer eating meat. They do not think in terms of great concepts of economic growth; they think only in terms of how much they can purchase by the end of the week at the market.
Therefore, 1 ask the Prime Minister in his visits and in whatever he does, not only to be present but also to be credible, and not to tie on a quick North-South visit through Africa and Brazil at the tail-end of a ski trip. He should make his efforts appear to be serious from the beginning so that the people who have never had the benefits he has can see that he is interested in them.
On the question of whether El Salvador is part of our responsibility-and we have spoken about that in the House this week-I would say it is part of our responsibility because it is our neighbour. If we do not have the ability to handle our responsibilities now, then I would seriously say that we must find a way to obtain it.
On December 4 of 1980, I wrote to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) a private letter which reads as follows:
I hope that you will be able to find a way in which Canada can protest against the whole situation and bring to bear some pressure that will amount to having the rights of the people protected. I know from some former correspondence and conversation with you that you feel that Central America is not really within the zone of Canadian influence. I hope that the position will change and that Canada will make a much greater effort in creating a policy which will show our support to the democratic forces which are being suppressed in these countries.
Present groups of delegates from these countries indicate how important they believe Canada is in their struggle.
I would suggest that you make a tour of that particular part of the world, with a strong emphasis on future contacts in Central America. I would like to see the question of human rights violations tackled in a more practical way.
I think we are at a stage in our history at which Canada can now begin to set up new relationships with our neighbours. We can now determine what kinds of relationsips they will be, whether they will just trail along behind a super-power which decides the future of those countries or whether we can go in as a neighbour and say that we want to be their neighbour and friend and that we would like to help. That would not be interpreted or understood as a power play to control the future of those countries but rather as our desire to see them develop in the way they want to develop.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
I would like to say much more, but I must close my remarks. Two years ago in February I attended the Latin American bishops' conference at Puebla, Mexico, when the Holy Father Pope John Paul II made his first visit to speak to the bishops of Latin America. While there, I was with the press corps and was standing beside Archbishop Oscar Romero when he gave a short press conference before he left to go back to San Salvador to bury one of his priests, who had been killed the previous day in an ambush by government troops. 1 can only remember it as being a highly emotional moment for myself and many who were standing there because we knew we would never see him again. He was going to stand tall for his people. In the following year, he came to terms with stress. A week before he was finally shot down by a long-range pistol bullet as he celebrated mass he said: "They can kill me, but the clamour for justice among the people they cannot silence".
I would like that to be my final thought and suggestion to my friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and to the government: let us stand tall as people in Canada. I know Canadians will support that. Stand tall, because the clamour for justice among the people will not be silenced.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-AMERICAN MILITARY INTERVENTION IN EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in the remarks tonight for just a few minutes to comment on how proud I am of the speeches which were made by individuals within my party, particularly the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) and the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle).
I was also pleased to hear some of the things said by members of the Conservative Party who spoke today, particularly the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I am pleased to associate myself with their remarks because they have expressed a feeling that I have about this country and about Canadians. That feeling arises from actions taken in the short history of this country in support of the rights of
March 9, 1981

others. Throughout our history, many selfless acts of support for others have been recorded. Indeed, in former times members of that party opposite, as the government, look positions that have made Canadians proud of their country.
1 was shocked, however, at the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) this afternoon who set out the role chosen by the government. I think it has lost an opportunity. Some hon. members opposite pointed out that they could not support the resolution. That is valid and I can accept their opposition to a motion which condemns the government's failure to act. But I felt that they failed to address head-on the question of the suffering, the termination of human rights and the murders going on in a very small country in central America. There was an implication that this country does not have an interest or expertise in that area of the world. There is a great deal of compassion in this country, however, a great deal of courage and a willingness to assist the people. There is also expertise and knowledge but there seems to be an argument regarding distance which is felt to justify this position.
1 think there is an important and profound role that we could play in such cases. Two countries seem to be in jeopardy at the moment, and we should speak out about them and the oppression they suffer. The first is El Salvador. Some hon. members said today that 5,000 to 6,000 children have been killed because they were suspected of being opposed to the regime. That kind of thing cannot be tolerated.
It is my understanding that El Salvador was run by an oligarchy of 14 families. They controlled the country for their own purposes. Some hon. members used an unfortunate description in their remarks today; perhaps the department wrote some of the speeches, they were so factual. They tended to point out what a great place El Salvador is and to make much of the improvements that have been made. I do not know who coined some of the phrases those hon. members used, such as "highly respected military junta". There might be a line of thought that says, "yes, Hitler did put everybody to work" or, "yes, Mussolini made the trains run on time." I do not think that it is a wise choice of terms, however. I do not think I can identify, nor should the government identify, with some of the things that are taking place in El Salvador at the present time, and I am a little confused by the position the government has taken in the last few weeks.
I have in mind a scenario that goes something like this: that at some point last month the Secretary of State for External Affairs was invited to Washington to have talks with General Haig. General Haig said, "Look, I would like Canada to make a strong statement in support of the United States supplying arms and of the U.S. role generally in Central America." Then the minister came home and made a statement about acquiescing to the United States sending in arms and advisers. To my way of thinking, that was wrong. There was an immediate vociferous reaction in this House.
Next day, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, a little more clearly, that he felt the Americans were making a mistake. As an observer of Canadian-American relations over
El Salvador
the years I have seen, as we all have, what has happened when Canada has tried to stand up to the United States. I wonder whether there was some instant reaction to the Prime Minister's statement that he felt the United States had made a mistake because, shortly afterwards, the fishing treaty was shelved, money was released in the United States for the Garrison diversion, the Alaska Gas pipeline was called into question. Today, again, we heard the acquiescent speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and tonight we have heard a range of presentations from the government side that point out all the positive things that have happened in El Salvador.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, it is one of the most destructive governments ever. As Canadians we should stand up and this government should stand up and condemn its activities. We should call for arbitration or mediation of the dispute and call for a halt to the supply of arms and military advisers.
The other country in Central America which I feel is in some jeopardy, and which has come through what El Salvador is going through today, is Nicaragua. I am particularly concerned about this after what occurred in Chile due to American influence. In that country, whether the Allende government was right or wrong, 30,000 people were murdered by a military dictatorship. I think we can lay the responsibility for that dictatorship in the hands of the United States.
In Nicaragua today, there appears to be a government which displaced one of the most reprehensible dictators in Central America, namely Somosa. It took a long time to get him out. The litany of death, torture and violation of human rights equals that of El Salvador. Today, however, the United States speaks of boycotts, accuses Nicaragua of shipping arms to El Salvador and speaks of a whole host of reprisals against that country. I feel, however, that the country is going through a process that will lead to improvements and to democracy. Forty per cent of the productive capacity of the country was stolen or destroyed by Somosa in reprisal; thousands of people were killed; the country was destroyed by Somosa, but today a five-man junta is rebuilding the country. It is going through the process of reconstruction and is committed to holding elections in 1985. Today I heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs condemning that process, saying El Salvador had committed itself to an earlier period for the election.
I submit that if we were to assist in that reconstruction process, if we were to support a government that is going through an evolutionary period and has overcome the violent revolution and wants to get on with rebuilding, probably the elections may come sooner.
It is my understanding that illiteracy stands around 70 per cent. Fifteen days after the junta came to power, it began a crusade against illiteracy and four months later thousands of young people went into the countryside to teach the people of Nicaragua to read and write. In some Indian areas, they invented scripts for languages that did not have written form. The next crusade was to improve health. In Nicaragua, people do not die of cancer, a luxury disease, they die of diarrhea.

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
They do not have a knowledge of standards of health and sanitation, and the next crusade is to improve standards of health and sanitation.
In the meantime, the United States started talking about boycotts, about intervention, about serious reprisals against the country-200 million people stomping on two million in a country just decimated by a vicious civil war and before that by a vicious dictator. This is one of the most outstanding examples of bullying and blindness in a long time.
When our friend, Mr. Reagan, visits us this week, we must convince him that what is needed in Central America is assistance in this evolutionary process of democratization. The greatest role we can play is to assist Nicaragua to restore its productive forces. We must assist with crusades for literacy, education, technical advancement and health. We must help to improve the lot of the people. Not only will Canadians-and Americans if they participate-win tremendous respect and support, but it would prevent a very tragic mistake from occurring which would draw more and more extremist forces into the Americas. It is interesting to think of the possibilities of an example such as Nicaragua. Certainly El Salvador is a different case.
1 saw the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) sitting in this chamber tonight. He is going through a buyback procedure to take fishing boats off the Canadian west coast. I understand Somoza stole and destroyed every fishing boat in Nicaragua along with many of the factories. I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries might be prepared to offer to the government of Nicaragua those vessels we want to remove from the Canadian fishing industry so we can assist that country. I wonder whether the government of Saskatchewan and other sincere people in the country might want to supply food to the Nicaraguans to help them.
When Mr. Reagan comes to Canada, we should try to help him understand our point of view. We should not fear standing up with courage and conviction as Canadians to explain to him how seriously we view these matters and how much we would like to participate with the Americans in the evolution toward democratization and improving the lot of people in Central America at this time.
I have heard people explain their contacts with the United States during this debate. I would like to explain mine. 1 have American friends and part of my family is American. My mother was born in the United States, and most of my cousins and my uncles and aunts live in that country. When I see the President of the United States, I reflect back to my grandfathers who fought in an active theatre of war in Europe. My father and uncles all fought in an active theatre of war in Europe. In my generation, I and my two brothers are the only members of the family since the turn of the century who have escaped serving in an active theatre of war. My cousins in the United States and my mother's family were not so lucky; they wound up in Vietnam fighting in an active theatre of war with
very tragic consequences. It tested their concern as Americans. They did not believe in what they were doing. They saw their country torn apart by a tragic mistake.
The acquiescent speeches given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs over the last few weeks remind me very clearly of the Vietnam experience and how timid and reluctant we were until the end to come out and say it was a mistake. By that time, most of the people in the United States had figured out it was a terrible mistake.
I do not see it as a thing of that magnitude. All I see is two million people who are very depressed and in poverty-stricken circumstances being turned back to the 1930s and the old military dictatorship and the banana plantations, with the support of the U.S. marines. We should not support that turning back of the clock even though it is at a different level. We should invite Mr. Reagan to join with us to stop the flow of arms into Central America to begin the process, which our leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), has suggested, of trying to reach a political solution to the problem of El Salvador and then becoming involved in Central America, in the development and enhancement of the lives of those people.
I do not mind the criticism of the resolution we have put forward, that is a point of view, but I would like to hear a different approach from that of government members in the kinds of speeches they are making, things which might track along the remarks made by my colleagues from the Conservative Party and my own party. I think Canadians want to hear something concrete. I have received a great deal of mail from members of churches in my community, members of trade union groups and people from all walks of life who want to see the government move in that direction. I know other members are receiving letters. This is a serious enough issue to which the government should respond in a way to meet the desire of Canadians and the way I think is traditional in Canada.
